speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister)1: Mr. Speaker, I desire to table the first interim report of the national capital planning committee, together with related documents and reports, with the exception of appendix 4 to the first interim report.
The present report of the national capital planning committee is an interim report dealing with two particular projects involved in the general planning of the capital. The first recommendation in the report deals with the acquisition of certain areas on the outskirts of the cities of Ottawa and Hull for industrial development purposes. The second recommendation deals with the construction of a new bridge across the Rideau canal, a,t a point about midway between Rideau and Laurier streets, in order to provide a new thoroughfare to relieve the present congestion of traffic in the area of confederation square.
So far as the first recommendation is concerned the proposal is to have certain areas
Capital Planning Committee

acquired by the government in order that they may be made available for industrial uses. A tentative recommendation with regard to the precise areas involved has been submitted on appendix 4 to the report. However, it is felt that on these details further study is desirable and, for this reason, copies of appendix 4 are not being tabled at this time. The appendix, or such modification of it as is finally decided on, will be tabled at a later date.
The broad purpose in recommending the acquisition of industrial sites is to enable land to be used for industry in locations where there would be no conflict with the general plans for the capital. These locations would be so selected as to make possible the ultimate removal of many of the railway lines which at present intersect the capital in such a way as to mar its appearance and to add to the hazards and congestion of traffic. The proposal is that initially the cost of acquiring the areas should be borne by the government. However, it is recommended that the property should be sold, over a period of time, to industrial users wishing to locate in the capital area, in such a way that the project would become largely or completely self-liquidating.
So far as the second recommendation, with regard to the bridge, is concerned. I believe hon. members who have had experience with the traffic congestion in confederation square and in front of the station will agree that something must be done a<t an early day to improve conditions. The proposal for the bridge appears to be a possible solution, and an item will be included in the supplementary estimates for $100,000 to enable preliminary engineering surveys and estimates of cost to be made.
I wish to emphasize that both projects which I have mentioned are at present simply recommendations of the national capital planning committee, carrying with them the approval of the federal district commission. Before any final decisions are taken with regard to them they will be given most careful consideration by the government and discussed in such manner as may be necessary with the municipal authorities involved.

The ship was purchased by a Canadian firm, was repaired in Germany and then moved to Britain for further repairs, and has now been delivered in Canada. The ship has been surveyed and is found capable of carrying 600 immigrants. The survey was made at the request of the present owners, who propose to convert the ship at their own expense for carrying immigrants. National Parks
The house resumed from Thursday, July 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe for the second reading of Bill No. 365, respecting certain national parks and to amend the National Parks Act.

This seems to be a sort of omnibus bill covering quite a number of parks. With some of the recommendations contained in the bill I can find no fault. Some of them are excellent, but there is one vicious recommendation, namely, the part which refers to the Prince Albert park. A measure having to do with this park was withdrawn in this house some six years ago.
I see no objection whatever, in fact I am quite in accord with- the recommendation to increase the size of the Fort Beausejour park. If I understand the bill properly, the land consists of twenty acres, and is being donated by Doctor J. C. Webster who is the chairman of the national parks board. If I might digress for a moment-
Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. gentleman. May I ask the hon. members to moderate their voices? It is almost impossible to follow the hon. member who has the floor.

I was about to say that the house and the country should pay marked respect to Doctor Webster for his great generosity in donating some twenty acres of land, as I understand it, to the country. If it can be done in any way that will be accepted, the house should pay that mark of respect to Doctor Webster. Fort Beausejour is a fine park and one that is visited by many tourists. The parcel of land which Doctor Webster has donated contains the site of General Moncton's lines of attack in the siege of 1775. That part of the bill I can very strongly support.
I see no objection to the part pertaining to Riding Mountain. It looks to me like an exchange of one square mile of land inside Riding Mountain park in Manitoba for a square mile of land on the borders of Riding Mountain park. I have been in Riding Mountain park on several occasions. In Riding Mountain park Manitoba has a magnificent area, but I should like to see it enlarged. I am sure that the people of Manitoba are delighted to have such a splendid park in their province, and I see no reason why the part of the bill having to do with this park should not be supported.
As I understand it the bill does not indi-83166-328
cate that any payment is to be made for this exchange. When the minister closes the debate I should like him to explain whether the exchange in Riding Mountain park is an exchange of 640 acres in the park for 640 acres outside. If so, whoever is responsible for the exchange should be complimented.
Elk Island park, which I have visited, is some distance east of Edmonton where we have many buffalo which belong to this country. That part of the bill I can support, because it increases the grazing area for the buffalo and the other animals in Elk Island park. I do not know why the government wishes to reduce Waterton Lakes park. I cannot understand it. If there is some legitimate reason for it I would not particularly oppose it, but that area of Alberta needs all the watershed ^of Waterton that it can get. The reduction will not be very large, some sixteen square miles, I believe, but we own it, and in my judgment, any reduction of the area adjacent to Waterton Lake will be bad for this country. It should not be supported. It is such a small matter that I am not going to carry on the debate too long. I should like the minister to look into that. I realize that the minister who is piloting the bill is perhaps not familiar with all these areas. I want to be as sympathetic to him as I can; I want to help him rather than to obstruct him. Waterton is a beautiful lake. I doubt whether there is a more beautiful lake in North America. These sixteen square miles adjacent to it have been used for the feeding of wild animals. We are now told that these animals are getting numerous. If we take this feeding area of sixteen square miles away from that area we shall be reducing the feeding area roundabout for the animals. If we do not have to do it, and if the public does not gain anything by doing it, if I were the minister I would oppose any recommendation to reduce the area around Waterton Lake.
Another recommendation of the bill has to do with the Nemiskam park and Buffalo park areas. I am not familiar with either one of those, therefore I cannot comment on them. Apparently these two parks are to be wiped out. Not having seen them I am not going to say anything about either one of these changes. If there is no reason why they should be kept, perhaps there is no reason why I should oppose their not being kept.
The next recommendation is one which I strongly oppose. I refer to the reduction in area of the Prince Albert park. The one province in Canada that has very little park area is Saskatchewan. I know of only two other Saskatchewan parks, one near the

National Parks

Cypress hills and the other around Watrous. The third is Prince Albert park. I do not know whether I have been to Prince Albert park. I drove northwest of Prince Albert for perhaps forty or fifty miles at the time I was making a survey of the watershed of the Sturgeon river. I was interested in that because during the Northwest rebellion the Hudson bay boats wintered at the mouth of the Sturgeon river. Years before that the Hudson bay boats traversing the Saskatchewan river wintered at the junction of the Sturgeon and Saskatchewan rivers. I like to see areas in which I am interested. I was interested in the history associated with the Sturgeon river. The Sturgeon river forms about one-third to one-half of the west boundary of the Prince Albert park.

I wish the hon.
member woud face this way. I cannot hear a word he says.

I had started to say that one reason I became interested in the Prince Albert park is that about one-third of the west boundary of the park is formed by the Sturgeon river. It is an historical river in that part of Saskatchewan. In the early days the Hudson bay boats wintered at the mouth of the Sturgeon river because of the water roads at the mouth of the river. During the rebellion of 1885 it played a small part in that rebellion.

The hon. member is
now discussing Prince Albert.

Yes: I believe the south boundary of Prince Albert park is about forty miles north of Prince Albert. I do not claim to know anything about the inside of the park, never having travelled through it. I travelled through much of the area east of it. I presume the area is much the same as the park itself. It is about fifty-four miles down the west boundary and about thirty miles across the top boundary; there is a large part of the park projecting about eighteen miles east of the third meridian, and that projection ranges about twenty-four miles north. It is that part, that eighteen by twenty-four miles, that the bill proposes taking off Prince Albert park.
It has been said, although I do not know whether the minister himself has expressed the same opinion, that that particular area is of little importance or value. Whoever says so, I would say that he is not at all familiar with the river watersheds in that locality. He cannot be if he feels like that. That particular 350 square miles comprise in the area which it is proposed to take out is, in my

judgment, a mighty important part of the watershed of the Montreal river which drains into Lac la Ronge and then into the Churchill river. A few nights ago we passed a bill granting $6,300,000 for the preservation of the watersheds on the east slopes of the Rocky mountains in connection with the Saskatchewan river. This strikes me as being the reversal of that policy, because we are going to throw away-that is all we are doing-an important part of the watershed of the Montreal river in that area.

I would point out that it is not proposed to alienate all the property in question from the crown. Part of it is being changed from a national park to an Indian reserve, on the theory that the Indians can make better use of it than the park commission.

I said I wanted to be easy on the minister because I know that he does not know much about the area. He does not administer that department, and unless he travels through the area he cannot be familiar with it. If he had travelled through it I do not think he would make that statement. This 350 miles, comprising between 75 and 150 lakes, is a very important part of that area. Two or three of these lakes are quite extensive. Part of the Montreal lake, which is a fairly large body of water, is also included.
It has been said that it is largely a muskeg area, but I must tell the minister that, next to a lake there is no part of the watershed that is as valuable to the river as muskeg. The other day the statement was made that the area was of little value because it was muskeg. Muskeg is of great importance to the watershed of any river, and I suggest that every possible effort should be made to preserve the watersheds of our rivers instead of throwing them open, I was going to say, to destruction. In fact, I think that term expresses it correctly, because as soon as this 350 square miles is taken out of the national park it will be denuded of forest. I believe there are a million and a half feet of timber on this 350 square miles, and that forest will be denuded if that territory is taken out ruthlessly.
I am not opposed to the taking out of timber that should be removed. The Ontario government is doing it in Algonquin park, but it is doing it under the instructions of engineers who mark the trees that should be taken out. I would not oppose trees being cut in that park by the government. The statement has been made that there are a million and a half board measure feet there. What I am opposed' to, however, since I have taken a

National Parks
great interest in the conservation of our natural resources all my lfe, is the ruthless destruction of any of the watersheds of any part of them. When this park was created in 1927 or 1928, those who undertook the work deserved1 every credit. I suggest, however, that if they had looked ahead they would have carried the line of the park right up the Churchill river and so created in Saskatchewan the largest national park in Canada. That is one province that should have a large park and there is little park area in southern Saskatchewan. There are only the two small ones I referred to earlier. This is a natural national park area and the part it is proposed now to take out should be retained.
I wish the minister could visualize as I do the effects of the proposal now before us. He would draw his pencil through that part of the bill without any hesitation. So far as the rest of it is concerned, it may not involve any great amount of trouble, but certainly that part of the bill is one that I shall oppose as strongly as possible and when we get into committee I intend to move a motion to throw it out. I shall do this because of the great value to Canada of all the head waters of the Churchill river. Up to the present little has been done on the Churchill river. As the minister knows, it flows into Hudson bay at Churchill. There is a large volume of water which, six miles west of Churchill, provides a fairly substantial power site. I have heard various figures mentioned-one million, two million or three million.
Every part of that watershed should be preserved for power purposes. I know that is only a small part of it, but many a mickle makes a muckle, and if this area that I speak of is destroyed, many other parts of that watershed will suffer likewise, and in due time we shall find ourselves faced with exactly the same situation as we have had to face on the Saskatchewan, being under the necessity of voting millions of dollars for restoration. There is no reason why we should have to do any such thing, because the country owns that area now.
This area does not play an important part inside the park itself, but it does possess the attribute of being muskeg, which preserves the moss, as muskeg does, for the feeding of wild animals; and, as the minister knows, that part of Prince Albert park is a breeding ground for wild animals in all that area. Moreover, east of this area, outside Prince Albert park, is one of the best hunting grounds in Canada, and certainly in the province of Saskatchewan. But the breeding grounds would be destroyed if the trees were cut down.
83166-328J
As I view it, it would be a retrograde step to take that 350 miles out of the Prince Albert park and I must protest as strongly as I can against the introduction of what I would call a vicious proposal, a proposal that was pretty well thrown out of the house six years ago. As a matter of fact, the bill was withdrawn at that time. I suggest that it should have been thrown out; it should have been kicked out, and I would like to see this particular part of the measure now before us kicked out at this time. In my opinion it is a vicious proposal to bring it in together with several good things we do not wish to oppose.
Why was not this Prince Albert park part of the bill brought in by itself? Some members may not wish to oppose it in view of the fact that it contains other features that they would like to support. However, as I say, when we are in committee we can move to delete this particular part.
I have travelled the area adjacent to it and I look upon all these areas as very valuable from the standpoint of the watersheds of our rivers. In this particular case, when you consider the Montreal river, the headwaters of one of the branches of the Churchill river, and appraise their importance to the country, I submit that it would be a retrograde step to take this territory out of the park area with the possibility of the timber being ruthlessly taken off and the muskeg being destroyed.
Someone will say that the purpose of the bill is to help the Indians. I am all for that, and if I thought the Indian would get any part of it I would say, yes, let the Indian have a part of it. But he will not get it. There are a good many halfbreeds in that country; indeed there are more halfbreeds than there are Indians. These halfbreeds as well as the Indians and the whites would have their rights there, because once you surrender title to it and it goes back to the province they can do what they like with it. In my opinion that would be very bad business.
The Prime Minister has a special interest in that park and I should think he would like to see it preserved. It was opened in 1927 when he began to represent that part of the country, and the people, out of respect for his great support in creating the park, presented him with an ideal cottage on the shores of Lake Waskesiu. I have heard it said that when you stand on the verandah of that cottage and look over the lake the scene is one of the most picturesque the eye can behold. If this part of the park is taken out it will seriously affect that locality.
If you take away two other small areas on the south side of the park, as is proposed- and it consists, I believe, of thirty acres more
National Parks

or less-and open it up to settlement, are you not going to invite a fire hazard into the park itself? I think we should make every effort to preserve that park. Saskatchewan needs it more than does any other part of Canada, but we all need it. What do we get out of any reduction of the park? We are told that we get a reduction of the cost of perhaps one or two fire rangers. But what is that? When this house cuts things down so small that it is going to throw away good park land for the sake of saving the salaries of one or two fire-rangers, it is getting down pretty small indeed. If we were so careful as that in the expenditure of all our moneys we should have today a surplus of hundreds of millions of dollars instead of what we have.
I would urge the minister not to let anyone convince him that the surrender of this additional thirty odd acres more or less, on the south side of the park, will be of benefit to Canada. It will not be of benefit to Canada. We do not have to surrender it and we get nothing out of it in any event. The same thing applies to the big eastern area. I want to plead with the minister as strongly as I can. He has heard me say many times that I have a warm feeling for him. He has done a big job. I have said that before. That is not flattery. I say to him: Do not let somebody come in here and tell you-and they must know you are not familiar with that area -to jam this bill through. Do not let anybody do that. The minister has done too many good things to be mixed up with a business like this; and I do not mean that he is mixed up in it in any way other than that the country is surrendering land which should be retained for park purposes, muskeg and trees, and for the preservation of the watersheds of the Montreal river. As one who has travelled to the headwaters of most rivers and surveyed their origin, I am intensely interested in their preservation. As far as the Montreal river is concerned, that 350 miles is almost priceless to its preservation. I know it starts in Waskesiu lake in the main park itself. I know it gets some of its water from Kings-mere lake, called after our Prime Minister. But a large source of it comes out of that 350 square miles which contain some 75 to 150 lakes. This is my last word. I know one thing. If the minister just sees the picture as I see it-and I have seen a lot of it-he will have the same opinion as I have, namely, that the watersheds of these rivers are priceless and should not be ruthlessly thrown away. We own them now and we should retain them.

Mr. Speaker, when I first entered the House of Commons in 1922 I brought to the attention

of parliament the great value a national and provincial parks system could have to the people of this country, from the point of view of preserving the regions named, of the beautification of the country, of health and recreation, and the providing of educational facilities and outdoor sport for all classes of our people. The bill before the house today is a limited one. Its purpose is to adjust the boundaries of four national parks under the general statute and also to close two others. The purpose of the bill is all right as far as it goes, but I desire to call attention to one fact. Part of the bill provides for certain social services, for health, recreation, and so on, which the people outside of the national parks system are given by the provinces. I would call the attention of the minister to one or two things about this policy. The principle of the bill is very largely what I wish to speak about. I remember years ago, when I first entered the House of Commons, I called attention to the deplorable condition of the battlefields and parks in the Niagara district. The house at Queenston Heights which was formerly the printing establishment of the Prime Minister's grandfather, William Lyon Mackenzie, was dilapidated, and the battlefields of the war of 1812 practically in ruins. My calling the attention of the government to that led to a debate in the house and later to a large expenditure by the Niagara Falls park commission and the rebuilding of the forts, parks and driveways.
How does it come about that this particular bill should be left to the hundred and sixth sitting day of the House of Commons? It deals with the important matter of the national parks system and the natural resources of this country, which are unsurpassed by those of any other country in the world. We should have had this up in the early days of the session. It comes up like external affairs estimates, in the dying days of the session. I do not wish to prolong the debate, but I want to say to the government that I am very much dissatisfied. I admit that little or nothing could be done during the war about this national parks system; the war was paramount. But now that the war is over-and it has been over for two years- there has been plenty of time to get on with the work and the programme and have surveys made in all the provinces. I remember taking this matter up, and set out in the explanatory notes, with regard to the two parks named. I have no objection to the policy or the principle of the bill, but I want to call attention to one thing. The province of

National Parks
Ontario, from which the present minister comes, is a forgotten province. I remember ever since I have been a member of the House of Commons that has been so. We see only five or six members from Ontario here today who are interested in a big matter like this. We have great natural resources in our province, in new Ontario, in the Rideau canal built by the British government in 1S44, the Trent canal connecting Muskoka and Temagami, lake Ontario and lake Simcoe, up to Severn bridge and beyond that, connecting with Georgian bay. We have a magnificent system of inland lakes and rivers in Northern Ontario and in the Peterborough district- Georgian bay, Parry Sound, the Nipissing district and right to the head of the lakes which the minister officially represents.
The general principle of the bill deals with the whole policy of a national parks system for the whole country. The act has now been amended three or four times; I think the last time was about 1941. As a result of the criticism I made in the house I was glad to see that the maritimes obtained some national parks in 1941. I have a list of the parks here. I will not refer to them, but they are set out on page 33 of the "Canada Year Book" and in the minister's annual report. The development of our national parks system was held up 'by the war-

Order. I would ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to the general principle of the bill. If he wants to discuss the general policy of the department, or part of it, he should do it when the estimates are before the house.

You are quite right, Mr. Speaker. In my opening remarks I said I was going to discuss the principle of the bill. The principle of the bill is all that may be discussed at this stage.
As I have said already, nothing has been done about the parks since the war, but I believe an interprovincial conference has been held within the past year or two with a view to coordinating the national and provincial parks. Surveys have been made but-aside from this bill nothing has yet been done. We in Ontario get no help at all, except in the Niagara district, from the province, and I call the attention of the minister to the lack of national parks in our province.
As to this particular bill may I say that I believe we have a great opportunity to make the whole of Canada like Switzerland, not only a huntsman's paradise but a thing of beauty and a joy forever. We have summer sports and winter sports, wild life, fishing and everything that could be desired-a huntsman's and fisherman's paradise. No other country in the world has such great natural resources; and instead of having these matters brought up in parliament in the last days of the session I hope they will be taken up at the coming interprovincial conference so that we shall get real value for the money expended on our park system. We are fifty years behind the times in catering to the tourist trade and developing our great natural resources.

I spoke on a bill similar to this in 1941, in relation to the Alberta national park; and I oppose the transfer of these lands from the dominion to the provincial governments at the present time. When the minister spoke on July 3 he said the land in question was not of much use anytway, that the land we were turning back or giving away wfas all muskeg. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) pointed out, however, that the muskeg was the water supply for the various lakes. From what I have heard and what I have been told by Alberta members I believe the dominion government is extremely foolish in turning back this land to the province of Saskatchewan. The bill states that some of this land will be turned into farms, which means it will gradually be encroached upon until there will not be a stick of timber left standing in the whole district. Even the timber in the portion the government intends to retain will be affected by the remainder of the land being denuded of trees, as will be the case, with the resulting loss of moisture. On June 24 of this year, in the other place, the minister who tried to pilot this bill through this house in 1941 said:
I recall being in the park in 1937, at the height of the drought in Saskatchewan, when everything was parched. I saw a farmer, his wife and three children drive into the park in an old model X Ford car with some provisions. They found a suitable place and pitched a tent to sleep in at night; and I thought what a wonderful thing it was that these people from the parched prairie country could come in and see evergreen trees and water and animals; and that, even if the park conferred no other benefits, what a boon it was to the children. This vacation feature is one of the great advantages of our park systems all across Canada.
In the estimates this year is an item of S650.000 for the tourist bureau. That money is to be used to attract tourists to Canada. If this bill goes through it will mean that on the one hand the government is paying out money to draw tourists to Canada while on the other hand it is getting rid of the attractions for the tourists. The minister knows that when they begin to cut trees eventually the pine, hemlock and spruce all disappear, because they
National Parks

cannot live without water. He also knows that if this land is turned over to the government of Saskatchewan, or any other government, who will allow settlers and Indians to go in there, eventually their holdings will be expanded into the present park so that before too long we shall have toother bill before parliament asking that another 373 square miles or more be removed from our parks. Just think what that means. The 373 square miles mentioned here would be equal to a piece of land a mile wide reaching from here to Kitchener, Ontario, which is a good deal of land. I plead with the minister to amend this bill by deleting that provision. Let this park remain as it is. It is foolish for this government to spend money to attract tourists to Canada and at the same time destroy the attractions that bring them here.

I am not familiar with the Prince Albert national park, but the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) made a statement opposing any reduction in its area, which I think deserves some reply. When we have once established a park I think it is a great mistake to cut down its area, unless there are very good reasons for doing so. However, I do not rise this afternoon to discuss that matter because, as I say, I am not personally familiar with the park. 'My purpose in rising is to join with the hon. member for Davenport in expressing appreciation to Doctor J. C. Webster and Mrs. Webster of Shediac, New Brunswick, for their very generous gift to the Dominion of Canada of over twenty acres of land, which will form an important addition to our historic parks. Doctor Webster, who was born in New Brunswick, for many years was a prominent physician in the city of Chicago, where he had an international reputation. When he retired from practice he returned to his native province, and since that time both he and Mrs. Webster have devoted a good part of their time and some of their wealth to its welfare. This gift he and Mrs. Webster are now making to the dominion is just one of many gifts they have made for the benefit of the people of this country.

I should like to add my word to the discussion of this bill, because I understand a certain portion of Waterton Lakes national park is to be cut out, with the net result that the area of that park will be reduced. I am not altogether satisfied with the reasons that have been given for taking out that portion of the park set out in the bill. Evidently it is not

a large portion; nevertheless there must be some reason for cutting it out. When the minister replies I should like him to give that reason, and the arguments in support of it. As a general principle I think we must take the attitude that we do not want our national parks reduced in size. If anything we want them to be extended or additional national parks acquired.
We have to preserve wild animal life in the mountainous regions. Most of the wild animals of Canada need plenty of grazing lands. Perhaps I could give an illustration. Banff national park is one of the finest virgin national parks in the world. There are a great many bear, mountain sheep, elk, antelope, moose, buffalo and other wild animals in that park, but I understand their number is gradually diminishing. They should be preserved. Banff is a great tourist attraction because the mountain scenery is simply magnificent. If tourists go to Banff hoping to see the wild animals of Canada they find that it is almost like looking for a needle in a haystack. They are there somewhere, but the park is quite large. Going into Banff you notice a sign with an arrow or hand pointing to the animal paddocks, but when the tourists go there expecting to see wild animals all they find are a few small mangy buffalo. The grass all over the paddock is worn and I am sure that tourists must get a wrong impression of the wild life in Canada. I do not believe that any other animals but buffalo are fenced off in the park.
If a tourist in Banff wants to see the bears he must wait until night and go down to the old stinking dump ground where they come in for their evening meal. There is no reason why a considerable portion of the park could not be set aside for bears.
In the southern part of Alberta, particularly around the Waterton lakes, there is wonderful mountainous country, although the scenery may not be quite as magnificent as at Banff, lake Louise or the Columbia ice fields. However, the southern part of Alberta is perhaps more prolific in forest growth and grazing pasture, and I believe plenty of room should be given to these animals. I know the department has spent considerable sums in Waterton lakes park. They have built a number of cottages and more and more people are coming to the park every year to spend their vacations. It is on the direct highway to the United States, and more and more tourists are coming from the United States to the park.
As a matter of broad principle the government should retain these parks and if pos-

National Parks .
sible make them larger instead of reducing their size. More money should be spent to make them real tourist attractions. On these broad principles I am afraid that I shall have to oppose the bill. I noticed from the discussion in the other place in respect to Prince Albert park that it was argued that the part to be taken out is of no use. I do not know whether that would refer also to the Waterton lakes park, but if it is of no use, what are you going to do with it? Someone will say: Give it back to the Indians. That is a nice argument-when it is of no use, give it back to the Indians. Or you may say: Give it back to the province. There is some reason for this government giving anything to the provinces.
If it is costing too much to maintain that portion of the park because of bog lands and the maintenance of highways, then is the government going to saddle the province with that expense? That does not make common sense and I do not think it is fair. As I say, on broad principles we shall have to oppose this bill unless the minister in charge can give a better reason for reducing the areas of these parks.

Mr. Speaker, in a general way I should like to associate myself with the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansel!) who has just taken his seat. One defect in this bill is that the ordinary member is not in position to know about the whole situation. I hope the minister when he makes his statement will clarify a number of matters which seem obscure to me. Waterton lakes national park is in my constituency. All that the hon. member for Macleod has said and a good deal more is true. I can understand how it might be wise to consider removing a certain portion of that park so that settlers could pasture their stock and so that timbering operations might be carried on, but I should like to know if there has been a demand for this from the settlers who live in that part of the park. Will the minister tell us whether Alberta has asked that this portion be taken out of the park, and whether the settlers nearby have asked for the same thing? Is it deemed advisable, in the light of these two circumstances, that a change be made in the boundaries of Water-ton Lakes national park?
I should like to ask two or three questions with regard to Prince Albert national park. This park is not in my constituency, but coming as I do from the west I am interested in it. Why does the government wish to dispose of an area from this park? The argument
seems to be, first, that it costs too much to maintain, and second, that it is not suitable for park development. What constitutes suitability for park development? How is it that the area which it is proposed to remove from the park does not qualify as suitable for park development?
There seems to be considerable uncertainty as to whether this area is to be added to an Indian reserve. I am not very much impressed by the argument that it is to be added to a reserve. I find in the explanatory note that approximately 373 square miles are to be removed from the park. If I read what is stated aright, only ten of the 373 square miles are supposed to be handed to the Indians to be joined to the Little Indian River reserve. If that is the actual state of affairs, it looks to me as though this argument about adding lands to the Indian reserves is unimpressive.
It is said that the cost of patrolling this parcel of land which it is proposed to remove from the Prince Albert park has been excessive in respect of looking after forest fires and the game. Will the minister tell us when he makes his statement what has been the actual cost of maintaining Prince Albert park during each of the last twenty years-he should have the figures-and what portion of that cost may be properly applied to the area which it is proposed to remove from the park? It seems to me that only by such figures can we form an estimate of the validity of the arguments in respect of the upkeep cost.
This whole bill and everything that has been said about this project up to the present time fills me with a considerable amount of suspicion. I had a good deal of suspicion in 1941 when the measure was brought into the house and I certainly have not had any of my suspicions allayed by reading what the Hon. Mr. Crerar had to say on this subject on June 24. It looks to me as though he was not very well informed about the matter and therefore not a very satisfactory witness.
I should like to read to the minister some of the statements that were made in the other place regarding this transfer of property, and ask him to explain away the statements that are made. I find that the Hon. W. M. Aseltine made the following statement as reported in the Senate Hansard of June 24:
An explanation given in committee was to the effect that there were some 400 Indians in the Montreal lake area, and that it was advisable that they should be given the right to trap in the area of some 350 square miles which it is now proposed to withdraw from the park.
Is it the intention to allow the Indians to trap over the whole 350 square miles? If
National Parks

that is the case I can see that there might be considerable value in making the transfer if the Indians could use all that land. But later on the hon. senator says:
. . . whether or not they would be the only ones allowed to trap in the area in question I learned that half-breeds and white settlers were also given permission.
If that happens, the poor Indians are not going to have very much chance at the game in this area. Further on he says:
It was added to the park originally for the purpose of preserving wild life, including muskrats, mink and all kinds of fur-bearing animals, particularly the beaver, and big game, such as elk, moose, and deer. It is known for a certainty that the animals we were hunting on the eastern boundary of the park were bred in that park and had spread throughout the surrounding country. This is particularly true of Candle lake, the home of the last surviving band of elk running at large in western Canada. That territory is their home ground, and if it is taken out of the park and thrown open to the public it will only be a year or two before all those animals are shot and killed.
If what the hon. senator says is correct, and the fact that he is from Rosetown, Saskatchewan, and states that he has been over the area concerned and has hunted over land contiguous to that area seems to make his words worthy of consideration, would the minister explain that matter to us also when he speaks? The hon. senator went on: The honourable senator has no idea how many hunters there are since the end of the war. During the war years all the young men were away but now they are back and are taking out hunting licences. They are allowed to go into this area. Even if the limit were one deer or one bull moose, it would only be a year or two before all these animals would be shot off.
I find myself strongly impressed by that statement because it is in conformity with what I have seen happen in parts of Alberta. Further on the hon.. senator said:
This land was set aside, not only as a park but as a place in which to preserve for posterity the wild life of that part of Saskatchewan.
If that is the case, certainly the reason for preserving the wild life of Saskatchewan must be just as strong today as it was when this land was set aside, and if the wild life of the dominion is to be preserved the dominion government ought to assume as much responsibility therefore as any province. The hon. senator went on:
The timber will be cut down ... I do not think the area proposed to be taken away is good for anything but park purposes.
That is widely at variance with the statement of Senator Crerar, who asserts definitely that it is not good for park purposes. How can any member be blamed for being com-
pletely confused over this matter when men supposed to know the most about the situation disagree so widely? When we have the hon. Senator Crerar, who was in this house as minister of mines and resources when the bill was introduced in 1941, and the hon. Senator Aseltine from Saskatchewan, who, by reason of his intimate experience with the park and the area in question, ought to know just as much about it as any other man, differing so widely, it seems to me that that is a situation which requires careful explanation on the part of the minister when he makes his reply.
The hon. Senator Kinley makes this statement in the Senate on June 24:
He stated that these Indians were not allowed to hunt in the park area, and that if this section was taken out of the park it would provide a source of livelihood for them. We hear a lot these days about the Indians, and what 'Canada took from them, and I think if they will live up in the north country, under such conditions as must prevail there, they should have the rights to any available hunting. We could very well turn the land over to the Indians.
The important aspect of that statement is that undoubtedly Senator Kinley was influenced to support the measure by the consideration that the whole of the area would be turned over to the Indians, when by the very statement in the bill itself opposite page 2, only ten square miles of this 373 square miles to be taken out of the park are to be turned over to the Indians. Surely there is something seriously wrong there. Senator Kinley went on to say, on the same page:
I said that if any land was available to the Indians we ought to let them have it,
With that I completely agree, and we should be sure before we take the landi out of the park that it will be turned over to the Indians. In the same discussion Senator Crerar said:
As a matter of fact, the greater part of the area is muskeg. A little bit is developed and might be salvaged by some small operations, but it is not suitable for park purposes.
What is the explanation why muskeg is not suitable for park purposes? I fail to see why it would not be. Certainly it is excellent land for the raising of wild animals and it is attractive from the tourist standpoint. There are muskeg areas over which corduroy roads have been built which constitute some of the most interesting scenery to be found in Alberta, and I take it that muskeg in other parts of Canada would be equally interesting. Senator Crerar went on to say:
The Indians will not have the sole right of trapping, but they will be assured of their fair share, and thereby a substantial means of livelihood will be provided for the band of Indians at Montreal lake.

National Parks
There again is uncertainty about this whole thing. It is said by some people that the Indians are not able to go in and hunt there today. As this area is part of a national park owned by the dominion I should like to know why the Indians should not be given access to hunting in that area. I cannot see why they should not be. Why should it be necessary to take this land out of the park in order to give the Indians a chance to hunt in the area? I shall say no more at this time, but when he makes his speech I would like to hear the minister's explanation of these conundrums.
Mr. D. S. HARKXES3 (Calgary East): Mr. Speaker, I agree with the idea which has been put forward by several hon. members that our policy should be to increase rather than decrease the area of our national parks. The decrease which is provided for in this bill personally I should be loath to vote for until we have had a much better explanation than we have had so far as to why it is necessary. That is particularly true of the Prince Albert national park and the Waterton Lakes park. I should like a better explanation than the one given in the explanatory notes as to the abolition of the Nemiskam park which was originally set aside to provide a refuge for antelope. It is stated here that it is no longer necessary to have a refuge for animals because they have increased materially during the last ten or twenty years. That is correct, but there is no guarantee that they will not be practically wiped out again, particularly with the increase in population in the southern part of Alberta and Saskatchewan owing to the development of irrigation schemes. Personally I think there is every possibility of these parks being required for the protection of animals again in the not too distant future. I do not want to hold up the business of the house and therefore will not press the matter now, but when we reach the committee stage we should have a better explanation of the sections than has so far been given.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Acting Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
As hon. members know, I am the acting minister of the department, and in that capacity can only convey the information which is given to me by the officers of the department. The officers of the department believe it is important that these amendments be made to the National Parks Act.
In the case of the Waterton national park it is pointed out that the sixteen square miles to be removed from within the present park boundary and transferred back to the prov-83166-329
ince lie in another watershed from that of the remainder of the park. The area of the Waterton Lakes park is considerable. The sixteen square miles is only a minor section of the .park.
The maintenance of national parks by the federal government is a considerable obligation. There are certain standards to be maintained. We have standards of protection and of development, and we have certain standards of improvements. As I understand the situation from the officers of the department, the purpose of the bill is to reduce the parks to an area which can be kept up to the standard set by the government for these national parks.
Before the .minister leaves the Waterton park will he answer this question, if the information has been given to him: Has there been a request on the part of Alberta-
I am told there has been.

And a request by
the settlers?
Through the province. I am assured that the province and the federal government are in complete agreement that the boundaries of the park should be altered as proposed in this bill.
That would carry a great deal of weight with me.

May I suggest to the
hon. member that he wait until we are in committee to put his questions.

The remarks I have just made apply only to the Prince Albert national park. The 350 square miles that are to be either returned to the province or added to a nearby Indian reserve consist of acres that cannot be kept up to the standard required in national parks.
Reference has been made to this being a suitable hunting ground for Indians. Hon. members will appreciate the fact that the government cannot allow hunting in its national parks and still preserve the game in these parks. If an area is to be hunted over it must be outside the park boundaries. Conversely, if the area is to be kept within the national parks it cannot be hunted over. It so happens that a fur conservation plan is in operation, in partnership between the dominion and the Saskatchewan government, in a nearby area. The purpose of the fur conservation plan is to provide a means of livelihood for a band of Indians on a nearby reservation, and for certain other settlers in the area. It

National Parks

is felt by both the province and the officers of the federal department, and by the government, that the well-being of the area will be better served by turning back the 350 square miles to the fur conservation plan, where it will be administered by the province under terms laid down by the federal government for a period of ten years, during which time its fur-bearing potentialities will be increased to the maximum possible. Ten square miles of the area is being transferred to the Indian reserve, and the remainder is being turned back to the province to be included in the fur conservation plan.
My purpose in rising, however, is to discuss section 9 of the bill. Section 9 is entirely new. At the present time the permanent residents in the parks do not receive the advantages of social services provided for other residents in the province in which the park i3 situated.
Order. I am sorry to interrupt the minister, but it is against the rules to discuss a section of the bill on second reading. I suggest that he wait until we are in committee.

It is not my purpose to discuss the section. This is a procedural point arising out of the fact that in the other place they decided that it was not competent to deal with one subsection, since it involved levying a tax. Therefore I find it my duty to ask for the unanimous consent of the house to introduce a resolution after second reading of this bill. After second reading I will move that the house go into committee on a resolution which will restore to the bill one subsection which was deleted in the other place.
Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

On division.
Motion agreed to on division and bill read the second time.

That the house go into committee of the whole this day to consider the following resolution:
Resolved, that the following provision he inserted as paragraph (p) of subsection one of section nine of Bill No. 365 (letter M-9 of the senate), intituled: "An act respecting certain national parks and to amend The National Parks Act," now before the house:
(p) _ levying taxes upon the residents of a park in order to defray the cost of health and welfare services supplied to such residents by a province pursuant to an agreement made under paragraph (o) of this subsection or supplied to such residents by the government of Canada.

He said: His Excellency the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the consideration of the house.

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, may I ask this question. Does the minister assume that the house concurs in the recommendation to add to section 9 something that will mean taxation on the residents of the park?

No. The purpose is to bring the section before the house for discussion and thus restore it to the bill. It by no means means an acceptance of the provision.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee on the resolution, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.

I move, Mr. Speaker, that the house now go into committee on the bill.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Additions to national parks.

I do not know what the proper procedure is, but I should think there ought to be some motion, or at any rate a letter addressed to Doctor J. C. Webster, C.M.G., acknowledging the splendid gift he is making to the country in connection with this important park. If his wife is associated with him in the gift, I suggest that her name be coupled with any such acknowledgment.

That has already been attended to by the minister of the appropriate department. The formal opening of the park was held and I believe that all honours have been bestowed upon Doctor Webster appropriate to the occasion. I cannot think of anything else, short of a vote of parliament, that would be appropriate.
It is fitting that the minister should have mentioned the fact in the discussion of the bill.

The minister assured us on the second reading that as far as Waterton park is concerned the province has agreed to this change. I would like to have an elaboration of that statement. How were the negotiations carried on with the province? Has the minister any correspondence in that regard? Perhaps I might add to the question. Is this parcel of land of approximately sixteen

National Parks
square miles simply to be passed over to the government of Alberta? Will they now be in possession of the land? When it is passed over to them will it be crown land in the right of the province to do with as they desire? I would like to know in what way the negotiations were conducted and whether there is any documentary evidence.
My hon. friend is not discussing section 2 at the moment.
That would come under section 5.
Then I will wait until we reach that section.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Land withdrawn from Prince Albert national park.

I would like to move an amendment to have this clause struck out but I am informed that I cannot do so. I would ask the -minister, however, to take steps to withdraw it, and if he does not care to do that then we shall have to ask for the yeas and nays. Before doing -that, however, I wish to say a few words to the minister. As I said at the beginning, I have a warm feeling for him and it is easy to see that he was not familiar with the areas he described in connection with Prince Albert park. I know he would like to set it right.
Reference w-as made to the muskeg area being the breeding grounds. That muskeg part, which is for the most part the 350 square mile area that is taken out of the park, is undoubtedly the breeding ground. There is no shooting there. No one can shoot in a national park and for that reason it is all protected breeding ground, so far as any government can protect breeding grounds. It is to all intents and purposes a protected breeding ground but the moment i-t is taken out of the national park area it ceases to be. The minister said that the province could see to this aspect of the matter. I do no-t know. Perhaps they would; on the other hand, they might not. The province will run its own show. Everyone with any knowledge of hunting in thiat area knows that i-t is the animals that are bred in that part of Prince Albert national park that move east, and every year there are hundreds of hunters who go out to that district to the east because they know that the animals are bred in that protected area.
The minister said something to the effect that if it were taken outside of the park it would become a potential area. That is what it is now. It is a real breeding area, as 83166-3294
a matter of fact. It is not simply potential, because it is in the park where shooting is not allowed.
Someone spoke about muskegs and it was said that muskegs will never be good agricultural land. If was not intended for that purpose at all. Something was also said about its reverting to the Indians, and I think the minister is under a misapprehension there. There might go to the Indians a small area of 10 square miles out of the 350 square miles in the eastern part of the park. Perhaps ten or eleven miles, I believe the description is, might be given to the Indians in Montreal river and Montreal lake area. But they now have the whole area north of that and to the east of it in which to trap and hunt. I still say .that should remain in the park, no matter what anyone advises the minister. As someone over here said, instead of taking that area out of the park, we should increase it by another 350 miles right up to Lac la Ronge if we can. We cannot have it too large in that country.
I should like to make my position quite clear. At the present time the 340 miles at present under discussion is in the park.
In that particular area.

Yes. Animals can breed
there; they cannot be shot.
That is where they breed.

In other words, it is just
wild land in which animals can breed. Both the provincial and federal government would like to include this land in a joint plan of fur conservation for which they have both provided funds. By arrangements between the two governments a certain area already has been set apart to be developed for fur conservation. It is a long term agreement, I think for twenty-five years. Each government has undertaken to spend a certain sum of money over that period in developing the area for the breeding of fur bearing animals. The purpose is to divert all of this area into the fur conservation plan, und-er this dominion-provincial agreement and to develop it as a fur conservation area rather than to maintain it as a federal park. As I say, all the officials of the federal government believe that constitutes a proper use. The province itself wishes to have the land transferred for the purposes of the other agreement, and I see no reason why parliament should not implement the wishes of those responsible for the development of the area.

A moment ago the
minister said ten years.
National Parks
I am corrected now by my officials. The period is twenty-five years.

The minister changes all
the time.

The minister said ten
acres. What the Indians are to get, if they get anything, will be near Montreal lake and will be approximately eleven square miles. I am sorry for the minister in his present position; I have the highest regard for our officials, but I lose my regard when I find officials in the parks department wanting to get rid of this large area of park land.
We are not getting rid of it.

Yes, you are getting rid of it. Do not take any stock in this idea that there is to be any cooperation with the provincial government. The provincial government has all the land outside of that and can start a park whenever it likes, the same as we have in Ontario. There is nothing in that. It has been going on too long. National Parks

I have no doubt it would be of benefit to some of the settlers in the vicinity, but I should think it would be of much greater benefit to the people of Canada as part of one of our national playgrounds than to turn it over to two or three people in the vicinity. I think probably it
will be found that an addition to the park can be made at the northern end, where there is a good deal of land which is not of particular value for grazing. There was no desire on the part of the province or anyone else to cut down the area of magnificent Waterton park, it was simply that the sixteen square miles would be a little more valuable if it were on the north end of the park where there are trees and mountains.

Do we need the consent of the United States before taking any land out of the Waterton Lakes national park? Have we

Some of it would be broken up and a good deal of the land would be blown away. This is in the part of the province which comes under the P.FjR.A. and I think it would be better for the dominion to keep it as a park so that it would be available in the future if it is needed for the protection and preservation of antelope. speechtext: Is it the purpose of the government to see that these citizens get these social services?

I am not sure that the question I want to ask comes under the particular item we are discussing.
For some time there has been dissatisfaction over conditions in our national parks, particularly in the Kootenay park and the Yoho national park. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO AGE OF RETIREMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a few words I should like to say about the measure that is before us, land I rise to do' so now because this is the only opportunity I shall have to bring to the attention of the house and of the government certain matters relating to pension and superannuation rights.
The bill before us calling for improvements in the Civil Service Superannuation Act has already received1 considerable acclaim. There may be some details concerning which improvement is desirable, but in the main the principle of the bill is highly commendable. The point I wish to bring to the attention of the government is that the considerations which they have found it desirable to implement in the case of civil servants are considerations which sooner or later must be implemented for all the people of Canada. This bill provides, for example, for mobility of employment without the loss of pension rights. In other words persons who have been working in other lines of employment with which pension rights were associated can now move into the civil service under certain conditions without losing the pension rights they had built up previously. It is also now possible for civil servants under certain conditions to leave the civil service to go into some other line of work and not lose their pension rights.
We also have in this bill a provision for definite recognition of the period spent in military service overseas so far as civil service pension rights are concerned. We have, too, a recognition that those who have been classed as temporary1 civil servants should be given consideration with respect to pension rights.
It is good to note the extent to which the principle of providing for security in old age is being recognized by the government with respect to the civil service and also to an ever larger extent by industry. We must not. however, lose sight of the fact that these various pension plans have to be paid for. That is true of any pension scheme, including old age pensions, which some of us advocate very strongly. The point I wish to make is this, that we are getting into a situation in this country where large numbers of people, rightly, are earning pension benefits portions of which have to be paid by persons who do not enjoy pension rights. When employees of an industry are earning a pension they pay for part of it themselves and part of it is paid for by the public who buy the product of that industry, and that public includes many people who do

not have the opportunity to provide pension benefits for themselves. And. so with civil service superannuation: in part it is paid for by the civil servants themselves out of their own remuneration; in part it is paid for out of the consolidated revenue fund, which means thait the taxpayers of Canada are helping to make it possible.
I want to make it very clear, Mr. Speaker, that I am in favour of all these pension plans, and I am pleased with the extent to which they are growing. But the fact is that they still leave out in the cold a great many other Canadians who do not have the opportunity to provide their own old age security and yet they have to help pay for the security of others. All of this means that the time has come in this country for parliament, and I say that because it seems to me that it ought to be a major plank in the platform of every party, to force whatever government is in power to move in the direction of a universal superannuation plan.
Some industries, for example the Canadian National Railways, already have in effect a plan whereby they give to their employees a certain gratuitous pension, a certain amount as a matter of right apart entirely from the employee's contributions; and then on top of that the employees receive a pension based on their contributions. I feel that the time is long overdue when not only the civil service but Canadians generally should have the benefit of some such plan. We should have an old age pension plan which provides the-basic minimum, but we must have in addition to it for all Canadians some such plan-

I know that rule, and that is the reason I am making these remarks on second reading. It seems to me that this' is the only place I can make them. I submit to Your Honour that the principle of this bill revolves around the extension of certain principles. These principles relate to making it possible for workers to move from private industry into the civil service or from the civil service into private industry without the loss of pension rights. The whole principle of this bill is to make more secure the old age of Canadian citizens both in and out of the civil service. It is not confined just to those who spend their lifetime as civil servants. The point I am trying to make is that the time has come when the government should bring before parliament a measure to provide'

Civil Service Superannuation Act
such over-all security for all the people. I am not talking about old age pensions as such; that is another matter. I submit that in, addition we should have a universal superannuation plan which should be, as this is, on a contributory basis. As a matter of fact it should go farther than that; it should cover all of the things that happen to people over which they have no control. I urge upon the government and upon this house the realization that there is perhaps no more desirable social objective toward which any party or any parliament or any government should strive.
We have come to the realization in our day and age that one of the things that our people need most is security; one of the things the lack of which causes so much hardship, suffering, frustration and loss of efficiency is insecurity. One of the shortest ways to offset all these evil things and to bring security into the Jives of our Canadian people is to give them the assurance that we are giving by this act to this group of people who having done their turn, having done their share of work in this country, will have at a reasonable retirement age, such as is now suggested in this bill, sixty-five or sixty, ample security.

speechtext:
Under this section I notice that the civil servant is to a large extent dependent upon designation by the treasury board. I believe that we should have gone a little farther and put into statutory form the various classifications of civil servants, because we can see gradually encroaching upon the civil service many persons who are not in the ordinary sense of the word servants of the government, but who are given equal status to career civil servants or permanent employees of various departments of government. For that reason I think it would be better for the civil service of Canada generally and for the civil servants themselves if the designation of a civil servant were put in statutory form and not subject to the ratification of the treasury board.
I can see situations developing by which persons who might be called secondary or third-class civil servants, members of committees, members of commissions, members of
crown companies, who are not in the same classification as the person who lends to the nation his talents and his abilities as a career or permanent civil servant, will encroach upon the civil service. They may be employed by the officers of a company, or by the heads of committees, on a temporary basis-not hired or fired, strictly speaking, by the government of Canada, but employed and discharged and given rights of salaries, superannuation and remuneration, leave of absence and so on, entirely apart from that set out in the Civil Service Act. I see a move on foot to bring these people into the same status as those who have given their talents, their ability and their education as a career within the civil service of Canada.
Generally speaking we Canadians are proud of the work our civil servants have done for Canada over the years. Their efficiency, their devotion to duty, their loyalty to the service is well known. We are not enhancing that prestige or increasing the efficiency of the career civil servants by adding to their category those who are not in the same status. In other words I believe that nobody should be given the classification of a civil servant unless he is employed under the Civil Service Act, with the rights, privileges, benefits and obligations common to the other ranks. It seems to me that we are going to see three, four or more different classes of civil servants under different terms of employment, with different rights and privileges; the treasury board-which is not known to the public to any great extent, and which varies from time to time, from government to government and from minister to minister-giving different rights, privileges and determinations as to their status. I do not think it is to the interest of Canada as a whole or to the civil service generally that this condition of affairs should prevail. I am disappointed that when the amendment to the Civil Service Act and to the Civil Service Superannuation Act was brought in, that line of demarcation was not put in statutory form instead of being left to the treasury board as at present.
In the employment of the government of Canada we have many people who have been temporary. I believe that by an amendment to the Civil Service Act they are to be made permanent. We do not know in what department, in what board, on what commission or with what crown company these employees are to be found who are to be accepted by the treasury board. Much advantage could be gained and much satisfaction given to the civil service generally if the civil servant were put into the class by statute rather than by- I was going to say the whim or fancy of

Civil Service Superannuation Act
individuals, but I do not like to use these words in a disparaging sense. It depends a good deal upon the representations made to the treasury board and the time at which these representations are made whether they are put in the classification.
Many of the civil servants appointed under the Civil Service Superannuation Act are making contributions to the fund equal to the amount paid by the government. They are now to see other classes come into the fund and draw benefits under conditions different from those under which they draw their benefits when they retire. It is not fair to the career civil servants. I would urge the government when dealing with the Civil Service Superannuation Act and the Civil Service Act to bear in mind that when persons are contributing to a superannuation fund, the fund should be earmarked as held in trust for the contributors and not dispersed in a manner which will be unfair to the career group.
Generally speaking . the people of Canada appreciate the amendments to the Civil Service Superannuation Act which are embodied in this bill. I am sure that there are many improvements in it which the civil servants and the people of Canada welcome. My learned friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre-

You have contributed to the fund, but if you leave the service you will not get the advantage of the security which you have been helping to build up". In my opinion this bill makes the fund much more flexible and more advantageous to the civil servants.
In providing superannuation for the civil service, we must not merely consider the inducement held out to capable persons to

join the service; we must consider the encouragement which is being given to the man who is doing a good job to remain in-the service, and security to him when he reaches the age of retirement forms a part of that encouragement.
These three points have, I believe, been thoroughly considered in this bill, and I commend these portions of it. I think, however, we could go quite a bit farther than we have in the directions I have indicated.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO AGE OF RETIREMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
I suppose it is well understood that members from the city of Ottawa or members who live close to Ottawa generally take an active interest in any bill of this kind, but to those of us who are not so close to the capital the picture presented is not quite the same. It is not the same as the picture painted by those who either live in Ottawa or live close to Ottawa and who depend upon the great vote of the civil service. I am not one of those who are against superannuation, but I am one of those who believe that our philosophy of life is all wrong. When you tell a person that he must retire at the age of sixty-five I think you are going directly against human nature itself.
Let me say to those who are advocating compulsory retirement at the age of sixty-five as a means of affording employment that they would do well to look up the figures, because if I were going to advocate anything from that point of view I would retire every one at the age of fifty. That is what I would do if my object were to give employment and a pension.
I say to hon. members who intend to vote for this bill that they had better also seriously consider their own position when they reach the age of sixty-five, because what is good for this group of citizens should apply to members of the House of Commons. I am not advocating it. I do not advocate it. I am one of those who think the best life for any man or woman, provided that he or she is in health and strength, the best life is one in which they can carry on as long as possible and is the life that will enable them perhaps to do their best work. Let us see what we are doing. We are making provision for this great class of citizens in the belief that we are doing it from a humanitarian point of view, whereas we are actually sounding the death-knell of the majority of these citizens. If you look at the figures in regard to those who are compulsorily retired at sixty-five years of age you will generally find that, once they quit, their length of life is, on the average, about five years.

Civil Service Superannuation Act
These people may have worked thirty-five or forty years; they have, during that time, had their sociability in their comings and goings among their fellow men; but one fine day the superintendent comes and says "Jack, it is too bad; next week you will have to retire". Then others go around the office and collect some money, and on Wednesday or Thursday or some suitable day the individual is presented with an umbrella or a fountain pen. Perhaps he has been looking forward to this day, saying to himself "Well, now I will enjoy life". But does he enjoy life to the full when he has nothing to do? If you live on the coast you may find them later sitting on benches along the shore with nothing to do. In this condition it is not long until the individual feels that he is the forgotten man.
I say to hon. members that we had better take more seriously what we are doing. The old country, I see, is now going to encourage its aged citizens to do some work, and so should we. Our philosophy of life is entirely wrong. However, I can understand members living in or near Ottawa extolling this bill. Bear in mind that I am in favour of superannuation, but I am not in favour of compulsorily retiring everyone at the age of sixty-five. Therefore, I would vote against this bill and not have it said of me at the age of sixty-five that as a member of parliament I should retire.
Is the usefulness of a man or woman gone because he or she has reached the age of sixty-five? What about Churchill? If we continue along this line we may soon find the man of thirty-five or forty pointing his finger at every one who has reached or is near the age of sixty-five and saying, "It is high time you quit that job and allowed someone else to step in." We are beginning to think-people are old and finished at sixty-five. I am not saying that those who are ill, those who may have been wounded in the last war and who may wish to retire, should not be allowed to do so. Provision might well be made for them to retire on a decent superannuation. But when you compel every man or woman of sixty-five and say to him or her "We have no more use for you; you must retire", then I warn those who contemplate the glory of this that they had better cultivate some hobby or other because when they are sixty-five and find themselves with nothing to do in life, they will not enjoy it as they may now think. The good Lord never intended it that way.
With things developing in this way, it is a wonder you can find any man or woman willing to work on a farm. They might very
well say, "Why should we put in long hours on a farm and receive no holidays or superannuation? Instead, we will go to the city or maybe get some government job."
Let me now take a minute or two to refer to a class of public servants about whom I have heard no word from any member of the House of Commons. I know I may not be popular in what I am about to say, and I may receive a lot of black looks. I do not want anyone to think that what I am going to say applies to all who work in the public service, because we have many public servants, here and elsewhere, who are working long hours and giving the best of their ability to their duties. But generally speaking, the civil servants in the government work six and a half hours a day, and then we turn round and say to the trade union men who advocate shorter hours that it cannot be done. I find some around Ottawa almost cursing the House of Commons because we are sitting. They say, "If you fellows were not talking so much we would get off at four o'clock." My heart bleeds for some of them working six and a half hours a day because I know that if we were out of here they would be working a full five and a half hours. They are entitled also to three weeks' holidays with pay, eleven statutory holidays and eighteen days sick leave. But that is not all. They are entitled to six days of special leave if someone dies in the family or if there is sickness; and some of them have the neat system of piling up days until they have accumulated 800 days of sick leave with pay.
They are getting all this with superannuation as well, for which the country pays half. As I say, they are in a special class, and yet we have a group of stenographers and secretaries around this building who have to seek jobs and have none of those advantages. I am not apologizing to anyone for saying a word on their behalf. In fact I would advocate a royal commission to look into all positions around this building.

These girls who work here will have to look for a position after the session ends. They have no superannuation. They have no sick leave. Their hours are long. As everyone knows, they work from nine in the morning till six in the evening, with an hour and a half off for lunch. Many, if not all of them, work in the evenings. There is hardly one who does not work one or two nights a week. Many work on Sundays to assist members, when required. I think most of them would rank as grade three stenographers. If they do not, it is up to the member to say whether or not they are capable.
