I am going to make this suggestion. I do not believe it would cost the country any more money to put them on a permanent basis by the year, and I shall explain why. speechtext: Would the minister state clearly the position as to superannuation of a civil servant in each of three classes: first, one who retires with less than ten years service; second, one who retires with more than ten years service but less than twenty years service and, third, one who retires with more than twenty years service but prior to the normal retirement age?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO AGE OF RETIREMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
The civil servant with less than ten years service who is retired by reason of age or incapacity is given the option of receiving a gratuity of one month's salary for each year of service or an immediate annuity reduced by one per cent for each year of service less than twenty. The latter is a new provision. In the case of abolition of office, there is the same option, a gratuity of one month's salary for each year of service or a deferred annuity reduced by one per cent for each year of service less than twenty. In the case of inefficiency,, he is given the return of contributions without' interest or the option of a deferred annuity reduced by one per cent for each year of service less than twenty. In the case of misconduct, there is no change; he receives a return of contributions without interest. When he is retired for other reasons, such as voluntary retirement, completion of a term appointment and so on he is given the option of the return of contributions without interest or a deferred annuity reduced by one per cent for each year of service less than twenty.
In the case of a civil servant with over ten years of service retired for age or incapacity, he is given an immediate annuity. There is no change from the present act. In the case of abolition of office, he is given an immediate annuity reduced by one-third to age sixty-five. There is no change there. In the case of inefficiency, he is given under the present act an immediate annuity reduced by fifty per cent to age sixty-five and 33J per cent thereafter. That is changed to a deferred annuity reduced by one per cent for each year of service less than twenty or withdrawal of contributions without interest, whichever he prefers.
There is no change with respect to dismissal for misconduct. The employee is given the return of contributions without interest.
For other reasons, such as voluntary retirement, completion of a term appointment, he has under this bill, if he has less than ten

Civil Service Superannuation Act
years service, the option of a deferred annuity reduced by one per cent for each year of service less than twenty, or the return of contributions without interest. If he has over ten years service he gets his full annuity rights, whatever they may be, reduced by one per cent for every year of service which is less than twenty, and at twenty years he gets his full annuity rights at the appropriate rate, deferred to age sixty years. whatever they may be. It may be that they have some blanket arrangement about expenses. I should like to know their actual remuneration and their basic salary in each case.

speechtext:
He took Mr. Justice Turgeon's place.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes, he replaced Mr. Justice Turgeon. Mr. K. A. Greene, who has just been appointed high commisisoner to Australia; Hon. T. C. Davis, now' Canadian ambassador to China and formerly high commissioner to Australia; Mr. Vaillancourt, Canadian minister to Cuba; Mr. Laureys, minister to Norway and Denmark, and formerly ambassador to Peru, and Mr. J. D. Kearney,, at first high commissioner to Ireland, then minister to Norway and Denmark and now high commissioner in India.
The others to whom the bill might apply, in meaning additional superannuation benefits to what they would be entitled to under other acts of the Canadian parliament, are Major-General G. P. Vanier, who is ambassador to France, and Major-General Maurice Pope, who is head of the Canadian military mission in Berlin; but with respect to Major-General Pope it would be only if the governor in council decided that the mission to Berlin was a mission comparable with ambassadorship or the office of consul general. Major-General LaFleche, ambassador to Greece; with respect to Major-General LaFleche, I am not in a position to say just what the effect would be. Major-General LaFleche was a member of the civil service for a number of years before he became a member of parliament and a minister of the crown; but he is not one who was in the civil service immediately before his appointment as an officer of external affairs. That is a matter that I asked to be given precise information upon, and have not as yet received information as to whether or not he would be entitled under the superannuation

act to superannuation benefits for the number of years he served in the civil service.

subsubtopic: PENSION OR SUPERANNUATION BENEFITS TO SENIOR APPOINTEES SERVING OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
If the gap between the time he was in the civil service and took on the job in Greece disqualified him, this bill would enter in.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: This bill would affect him just as if he had never been in the civil service, but only, of course, upon the conditions prescribed in the bill; that is to say, had the period of service that the bill calls for. When we come to the appropriate section it is my intention to ask that an amendment be moved to make sure that no one, no matter what his service may have been, can get more as a consequence of this bill than the maximum that this bill would provide if he had nothing else. Under this bill no one can get more than thir-ty-five fiftieths or seventy per cent of his salary. If a man was entitled to a superannuation benefit of a certain amount under another act of the parliament of Canada and by application of this bill got another allowance, the additional allowance will have to be cut down so that the two together will not amount to more than if his whole service had been in external affairs.

subsubtopic: PENSION OR SUPERANNUATION BENEFITS TO SENIOR APPOINTEES SERVING OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
He will not get two rates.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No. He will not be allowed more than if his whole period of public service- had been service with external affairs.

subsubtopic: PENSION OR SUPERANNUATION BENEFITS TO SENIOR APPOINTEES SERVING OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Now, the salaries.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The salaries are

Is it $10,000 each?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes; each of these heads of missions receives a salary of $10,000. Then, along the line of the previous question, Warwick Chipman, for instance, gets $10,000.

What has always concerned me is this. These judges are, so to speak, seconded from the bench for the time being into the diplomatic service. Do they not get some special advantage over others, or do they get the same as other people? Actually, under the changes in the Judges Act last year, I should think Mr. Justice Davis would be entitled to more than $10,000. I do
not know about Mr. Justice Turgeon. Does he get more than the others, or are they all on an equal basis?
Mr. 8T. LAURENT: All on an equal basis. Mr. Justice Turgeon had retired from the bench before the Judges Act was amended.

What about allowances?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Allowances are not counted for pension purposes, with just one exception. If a civil servant under the superannuation act is appointed head of a mission in external affairs at a salary that is less than would have been his salary in the civil service, under the superannuation act, the governor in council can, for the purposes of his continuation under the superannuation act, deem as part of his salary enough of his allowance so as not to prejudice him. That was particularly brought to our attention in connection with the case of Mr. Fraser Elliott, who accepted' a position in external affairs at a salary of less than his salary in the civil service, and he was informed that I would ask parliament, in dealing with this bill, to make provision whereby enough of his allowance might be deemed salary so that the change in salary would not affect his pension rights, although he would have to pay the contribution on the portion of the allowance that was for that purpose deemed salary. I think that is the whole scope of the bill.

I want to take advantage of clause 1 of the bill to make a reference to those honourable gentlemen who are serving us so well so far away from home. They are great citizens, great Canadians. During the war particularly they put enthusiasm, vigour and understanding into their work and it was my privilege to observe them in action.
I do not like to single out any particular name. I have not had an opportunity during the last two years to make the observations which, with your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should1 now like to make. I would mention Major-General Vanier, who, exiled to Algiers at the time I had the privilege of being a guest in his temporary domicile, did everything that he could possibly do on behalf of a Canadian, burdened though he was with, war cares.
In other parts "down under" we received similar consideration, and I have no criticism whatsoever to offer with regard to those names that have been mentioned. Most of the persons in question I have had the privilege of meeting, and I pay the highest tribute to them as great Canadians away from home doing a great job on behalf of Canada.
External Affairs

With your permission, sir, I should like to add one further tribute to the families of these gentlemen, to Madame Vanier and Mrs. Davis. These ladies, in their own way, made things pleasant to persons who were strangers to them, yet at the same time Canadians. To their guests they were as Canadians to Canadians. They went out of their way to do things, and I consider it my duty as well as a high privilege to pay tribute to our Canadian ambassadors-call them what you will- and their families away from home for making us feel at home when we ourselves were away from home. In the last two years I have been anxious to make this statement.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I wish to express my sincere appreciation of the words which the hon. member has spoken and which, we all know, are fully deserved by those who are doing their best to serve Canada's interests abroad, and by their families who are assisting them in every way possible and in an efficient manner.

I wish to get some information about these various excellencies because I have objected for years now to the extension of- the ambassador, minister, consul general and high commissioner principle. I have great admiration for the present minister, but I must object to voting money for ambassadors of one sort or another all over the seven seas. They have no knowledge whatever of external affairs. They learn by experience only. Even Solomon in all his glory was never arrayed like one of them; and, to refer still further to that passage in Scripture, "they toil not, neither do they spin." The thing is becoming ridiculous for a small country, and I think we had better get out of it. What have we in this department? We have a large number of these excellencies all over the globe. We have men in China and Japan, and before the war we had Hon. Mr. Bruce and, after it, General Odium. Now we have Judge Davis, who has been in Australia. He has been all over the world, on all the seas.
What have these people been doing except fostering the separatist tendency all over the empire and dividing Britain's representation? We have public officials called ambassadors; we have high commissioners; we have consuls general and all that kind of thing everywhere; to such an extent has this system been developed that their excellencies are beginning to make a laughing stock of the country, by so many of them being sent to great and small countries all over the world. That is the plain truth, if you ask me. For a country of ten and a half million people we have altogether 
too many of these useless representatives abroad. There is nothing but duplication and more duplication all along the line. There are officials under this department who do work overlapping that of the trade commissioners, agents and other officials of Canada. I have a splendid book on the Department of Trade and Commerce giving a list of countries, cities and towns where there are trade agents, commercial agents and so on. Some provinces and many businessmen have associations over there also. All this, in my opinion, is unnecessary duplication. If it were necessary I would not say a word, but are all these people necessary? No. What do they do? Nothing that I know of but get the country into trouble making speeches in foreign countries which they have no right to make. A lot of them are in uniforms. One landed in India the other day. He was formerly in southern Ireland. Now he has gone to India, and there were profuse articles about him and his uniform in the public press. And what about the staffs that assist these gentlemen? You have a first secretary, a second secretary, a third secretary and a fourth secretary; there is a secretary to the fourth secretary, and in addition to that this particular gentleman has a military staff with him to accompany him on land, in the air and on the sea, as he moves from one place to another.
Since I have been in the House of Commons, there has been discovered one great basic industry in Canada, located in the city of Ottawa, known as the ambassador cure for unemployment. I call it the ambassador cure for unemployment, for that is the only object I can see in it. Apart from that, they are doing nothing at all. They are of no value to Canada or to the Empire that I can see. We are talking about our status all the time, our autonomy and our sovereignty. Well, the status we had at the time of the last war, the sovereignty we enjoyed then, saw us through that war and another, in which thousands upon thousands of our young men were killed, and thousands upon thousands of others wounded. If that status was good enough for us then, it ought to be good enough for us today and especially for those of us who stayed at home. We should not be wanting to roam the seven seas.
We are fortunate that the position of the United States is far different. As a great ambassador or a great president of France said

I refer to Clemeneeau-Britain and the dominions were the hardest countries in the world to make a treaty with. Why? Because they did not speak with one voice

External Affairs
as the United States does. Fortunately in the United States there is one federal authority in control and not forty-eight separate states, each with ambassadors all over the seven seas. I do not mind the hon. member for Carleton supporting the measure as he does, because he is no doubt able to get some employment out of it, as are all the members for Ottawa city and Carleton county; although I do not think he has in his constituency any of these gentlemen who are roaming all over the seven seas.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Withdraw.

I think this has gone far enough. For example, when you look at the large powers such as Britain and France, and the others, how many ambassadors have they? The other day I saw a return, I think it was in British Hansard, which indicated they have only nine ambassadors. We have about twenty, if you ask me. I had a list of them which was in a return to an order of the house, giving their names. One would think we were a first-class power with 100 to 180 million people, having all these people roaming around on Cook's tours, par excellence and de luxe all over the seven seas learning the embassy business by experience. Everyone wants to be an ambassador. The hon. member for Vancouver South would qualify as an ambassador. He would make a very good one, as would many other hon. members. The hon. member for Temiscouata -he is not here today; he is taking a holiday -may be an ambassador some day. Some not only want to send ambassadors to various countries, but want to extend it to religious denominations. Some want to go to Canterbury cathedral and no doubt represent their denominations. Some want to go to Rome. Some want to go to the Church of Scotland where the hon. gentleman opposite-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I beg the hon. member's pardon; I belong to the Free Church of Scotland, not to the Church of Scotland.

I should like to say to Edinburgh's most distinguished graduate, that he would make a good ambassador of the Free Church of Scotland. I have seen him doing ambassadorial work on many occasions in the house, and he is a competent ambassador.
With all due respect, .Mr. Chairman, for a country with eleven to twelve million people I think we are going much too far with these vast expenditures. No doubt the pension is contributory. A man shall have to serve for five years first. But not one of them stayed five years in Australia; not one stayed more than one year. There have been three of
them down there, and now they are off to South America, and all that kind of thing. We are going too far. There is no public opinion to maintain this. In my opinion we are making a great mistake and causing separatism.

In what I have to say I do not wish to be considered as unappreciative of the services our representatives abroad are rendering to Canada, but I believe we should have some sense of proportion in these matters. Last week or the week before, we were considering pensions for people who have served this country as citizens, people who have given a lifetime in the service of the country. The conclusion this house came to was that our old age pensioners, man and wife, can live on a pension of $360 a year. I do not see how we can harmonize the provisions of this bill with what we did last week or the week before with regard to old age pensioners. For that reason-and I am speaking for myself and myself only-I intend to oppose this measure.
Daily I receive letters from constituents, indeed from people in all parts of Canada, who have to live on the war veterans allowance; and, mind you, they, are not people who have taken a pleasant and easy job at a good salary, but people who risked their lives for Canada. I had two letters today, one from an elderly couple who have to live on $60.83 a month. The man is not able to work. This man risked his life for Canada. Before we pay pensions of the amounts mentioned in this bill to people who have given only a few years' service, I think we should give more consideration to our senior citizens and to those who are now on what we call the burnt-out pension. We are told that we cannot do it, that the country cannot afford it.
Last year in the Judges Act there was provision for a pension for Mr. Justice Davis. It did not go through. Now we find that a completely new bill can be brought into this house for the purpose of providing a pension for one individual; that others come in on it is merely incidental. I jus!t cannot understand people who are fair-if my hon. friend wants to say something, let him get up and say it and stop murmuring while I am talking.
I just said I did not want the hon. member to be looking at me and preaching to me.

I am not looking at the hon. member; and if he did not look at me he would not notice that I was looking at him even if I were. But as I said, I cannot
External Affairs

understand how intelligent people, people who believe in equity and equality, can do this kind of thing. How can we explain it to our constituents when we go back home? How can I meet an elderly gentleman and his wife, people who have given their all in building up Canada and who are now told that they must live on $360 a year, when we have pensions of these amounts for others which we approve? Personally, I do not believe that those covered in this bill are any more entitled to the pension than is a member of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We do not get any, though.
They have not sacrificed nearly as much.
Not half as much.

I doubt if they have given any greater service to the country. I should not like to be personal in this matter, and I hope the hon. gentleman will not mind my saying this, but I believe the Minister of External Affairs himself is just as much entitled to a pension. I may be wrong, but I am of opinion that he undertook his present work as a duty to the country rather than from a desire to engage in politics. I appreciate that and honour him for it. That being the case, he is just as much entitled to a pension as are those who serve our country abroad. If you were to bring it down to that, all members of parliament are entitled to the same consideration. So far as I am concerned, I intend to oppose this and every similar measure until we deal with greater equity with the common, ordinary, citizens of Canada.

Will the minister explain to us what he means in section 2 by "such other persons of comparable status"? In the section he has already named the ambassadors, ministers, high commissioners and consuls general.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I shall be very glad to do that on section 2, if section 1 is carried.

In his remarks as to the advisability of proceeding with such a measure, the hon. member for Vancouver East raised one question in my mind. Did any of these appointees enter the service with any guarantee or assurance or undertaking or promise, direct or indirect, that they would get the advantage which this measure would seem to provide? I think that is an important point, because, after all, if they came in on the understanding that they would get $10,000 a year I am not sure that there is any 
need to give them something further, particularly if it applies only to one man. I do not know whether it applies to more than one, but at the moment the minister would seem to be a little concerned as to whether it does apply to more than one. I should like that point clarified.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: At the moment I am not sure that it even applies to one; I am not sure that Mr. Justice Davis has been five years in the service of external affairs. I do not think he has. He was in the Department of National War Services until nearly the end of the war. The other question must be answered in the negative. These gentlemen who were appointed to external affairs during the war accepted the appointments as a matter of public service to be performed for the country. Some of them were not inclined to continue. They were told that for persons brought in from outside the civil service it was intended to ask parliament to vote pensions which would be somewhat similar to those paid members of the judiciary. No bargain was made with anyone. I would not think it would be proper for me as minister of external affairs to make any promise as to what parliament would do about salaries or pensions. I do remember speaking to two or three and telling them it was my intention to ask parliament to enact a measure of this kind. I did not get the impression that had I not told them this they would have insisted upon retiring, but it came up in the course of conversations as to whether or not they would continue in the service. The only person to my recollection who was much concerned about this was Mr. Fraser Elliott, because he already had superannuation benefits and did not think it would be fair to ask him to abandon those benefits to serve in another capacity. I did tell him that I was going to bring this bill before parliament, that I hoped parliament would adopt it, and that if it were adopted I would ask that there be a provision in the bill which would permit him to continue making contributions based upon an amount equal to the salary he would have been receiving had he remained in another branch of the public service. But as far as my recollection goes, and I think it is pretty clear, that is the most that was done.
I did have some conversation about the matter with Mr. Justice Davis. I told him it would be contributory, and that to have the benefit of the years since he was first appointed to the bench there would be arrears of contributions to be paid. I asked to have a calculation made of what that would be, and it amounts to something close to $5,000. I did tell him that he would be required to pay

External Affairs
that amount if he wanted to get the benefit of the years which have elapsed since his appointment to the bench; but it did not go beyond that. It was something spoken of in the discussions we had about appointments to these offices.
I clearly remember that when Mr. Chipman was first appointed it was understood that he was being asked to serve during the period of the war; and the same was true when Mr. John D. Kearney, Mr. Ralston's former partner, was appointed. Then, when the war was over and it was found that they had performed what we looked upon as valuable service they were requested to remain, and were told that I was going to bring a bill before parliament containing provisions of this kind. But no agreement was made with them that their resignations would be accepted if the bill did not go through.

These twelve cases stand on a little different ground from what would be the case if they had been appointed under normal civil service arrangements. Reading some history of cases that occurred before I was in public life at all-perhaps things have changed since then-I find that sometimes when governments change some of these men are changed. I should not like to hold out either the hope or the threat that such things would happen if the government were to change again, but just suppose a future government was of a similar mind to past governments, shall I say. What would happen in the case of any of these men who might be removed on the same grounds on which other people have been removed? What would happen to the superannuation in that ease; because the bill only calls for retirement or resignation of a public official.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If that happened there would be no pension payable under this bill unless the one who retired came under the conditions set out in section 3: if he had attained the age of sixty-five and had served for not less than five years, or if he had become physically disabled from continuing to serve. Otherwise it would not apply; and that was frankly stated to these gentlemen. I think they all realize that situation.

There is nothing in this bill, as I see it, that would prevent a succeeding government from removing any of these people.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Oh) no; and there is nothing in this legislation that would give them an indemnity if they were removed. That was fully realized by all those with whom I discussed the terms of the proposed bill.

I do not want to delay the passing of section 1. While agreeing that the observations of the hon. member for Vancouver East contain a good deal of merit, personally I cannot feel that opposing this bill would automatically bring justice to these other groups he mentions. I am one of those who believe that anyone performing a service, outside Canada or within Canada, should be adequately compensated for service rendered. However I say that, by virtue of the government bringing in this bill, and by virtue of the party on the other side supporting it, the government is placed under a greater moral obligation to give justice to the other groups referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I shall not oppose the bill, but certainly I shall feel that I have a greater argument to use in fighting, for justice to the recipients of war veterans allowances, to our older persons and others within the country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would remind the committee that the principle of this bill was accepted by the house on second reading and that discussion should now be directly relative to the section. Most of the discussion that has taken place so far would have been more appropriate on second reading. Could we carry section 1 before six o'clock and then proceed with section 2?
Section agreed to on division.
On section 2-Definition.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I have an amendment which I will ask to have moved to add certain words to section 2, and I want to answer the questions put by the hon. member for Carleton.

After Recess

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
When the committee rose at six o'clock it had just passed clause 1 and we are now on clause 2.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Carleton had asked me. la question on clause 1 to which I promised an answer when we got to clause 2. It was with respect .to the words "and such other- person of comparable status serving in another country in the public service of Canada as the governor in council may designate". The hon. gentleman asked me what that might apply to. The words were inserted so that, in -the event of its becoming necessary for Canada to have a permanent representative at the seat of the
External Affairs

united nations, that permanent representative might, if the work he was doing there was of similar importance to that performed: by an ambassador, be designated as coming under the clause. It was felt that might be necessary because it is not ait all improbable that, in the event of Canada having to have a permanent representative at the seat of the united nations, someone now in the service of external affairs as ambassador might be designated to fill that office.
The question also arose as to whether the office at present occupied by General Pope at Berlin should be included. As a matter of fact, until very recently General Pope was a member of the permanent forces, seconded to the Department of External Affairs, and for that period would not, of course, even if he were included, derive any benefit from the bill. The post was not expressly mentioned because it may very well be that it will be only of quite short duration. It was thought that in bringing the bill before parliament there should be the possibility of including such officers of external affairs as might be heading the kind of mission we have had in Berlin or the kind of establishment we might have to have at New York or Lake Success to represent us in the organizations of the united nations. But thait will not necessarily be so, and if we put in precise language it might extend to more than w'ould be the intention of having it apply to. That was the reason for putting those words in. It was felt that in a case of that kind consideration should be given to the specific circumstances and that there should not be an attempt to cover it by general language which might include other than those it would be felt necessary or proper to include.

Might I ask the minister apropos of his suggestion that, as time goes on, it may become necessary for Canada to have permanent representation at the seat of the united nations, is that an immediate prospect, or does the minister envisage it more particularly if, as and when-and may I emphasize all three words-we become a member of the security council?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: What we had in mind *was that if, as when we become a member of the security council, the charter requires, as the hon. member knows, that every member on the security council shall have-a permanent representative at the seat of the organization.

I appreciate what the minister says, and probably his argument is sound that if we have the head of a military 
mission in some of the occupied countries he would be performing work similar to that of an ambassador, or if we had a representative at the united nations organizations with some permanency about his appointment the holder of that office would similarly merit superannuation as much as a diplomat. But both these cases are problematical, and the wording of the section is "such other person of comparable status serving in another country in the public service of Canada," and the governor in council is given pretty wide scope there to decide what other offices have comparable status to that of a diplomat. Only a five-year tenure of office is required until they become entitled to some pension. I do not want to speak on the next clause, but generous provision is being made, and it is within the realm of possibility that someone might be able to get this generous treatment that is meted out only to our diplomats. I think, therefore, we would be well advised to wait until the occasion arises, when an amendment could be made to the bill, rather than to leave it in fairly general terms as it is now. Would the minister consider restricting it to the position of ambassador, minister, high commissioner or consul general, and then, if the occasion arose within the next five years, an amendment could be made to the bill.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I think it is pretty closely restricted already. It says: "such other person of comparable status serving in another country in the public service of Canada". The hon. member says that the tenure may be only five years. But that, of course, applies only when, after five years, one has reached the age of sixty-five or has become physically incapacitated. who served overseas for five years or more. To my way of thinking, the senior officers of the armed services rendered a far greater service to Canada than any of these diplomats did.
In this connection the name of Major General Odium comes particularly to my mind. Along with some twenty thousand other Canadians I had the misfortune to serve under his command in England.

That is a nasty remark.

Personally, I think we should strike out of the bill subsection 2 (a) which provides for pensions to men who have served for between five and ten years. He is one of the most, gentlemanly of men, as Christian a gentleman as ever lived. He is a grand and gallant soldier. He is a splendid fellow. He is a true Canadian through and through, and I resent, with, all the resentment that my Highland emotion can command, the hon. member for Calgary East having the supreme effrontery to attack a bigger and. greater man.

Mr. Chairman, the

In other words, in this section we are providing for benefits by way of superannuation to any man, from the time he is sixty-five years of age, at $3,000 per annum, even though he has not served Canada in the diplomatic service, or anywhere else within the public service, for more than five years 83166-330J
prior to that. My own frank opinion is that we should appoint to the diplomatic service the best men in the country who will be an honour and a credit to Canada, and that these men should have some security when they leave their private vocations to enter that service. I do not believe that any man reaching the age of sixty or thereabouts and desiring to serve for five years, anxious to serve his country well for a short period of five years, would demand a pension for the rest of his life for doing so. I do not think it would be fair to the service generally, to the men in the Department of External Affairs and in the government service at large, who have spent a lifetime in acquiring knowledge, experience and the necessary ability to represent Canada abroad. On retiring on superannuation, they would realize that they could have worked almost their whole lives in their private vocations and could then have spent five years in the public service and obtained superannuation to this extent.
I agree entirely with the hon. member for Calgary East when he says that the minimum length of service for anyone in a diplomatic post, if he is to be entitled to a pension, should be ten years, if not even more. Then he has been away from his country and his: vocation and he does want security when he comes back. But a man who has been in business, commercial or professional life for a great many years, acquiring for himself the necessary qualifications for a diplomatic appointment-, will not accept a job for five-years by any inducement that may be held out in the form of a superannuation of $3,000 a year after that.
Bear in mind that people who have served' ten, fifteen or twenty years are contributing six per cent of their salary, a material amount, towards superannuation, whereas the man who has served for only a few short years pays only a small percentage of his annual salary. There is very little of the merit eii the contribution element in that aspect of it. I believe there are occasions when the superannuation provision may secure the services of men highly qualified for a diplomatic post, if they need it. But bearing in mind the many people in the Dominion of Canada who have not available to them any superannuation scheme, 1 do not believe we would be justified in saying that men getting a salary of $10,000 or more and serving for a short time, should get this benefit. I am sure the civil service generally will receive with approval most of the amendments contained in this bill, and I do not think I need dwell upon it at any length. Section 1 deals with definitions, and in particular deals with the extension of certain preferences to war veterans. In checking it over, I do not find that the section takes into consideration many who went overseas, not as members of the army, the air force or the navy, but who, I believe, should have the benefit of the veterans preference in the civil service. I speak particularly of such groups as the merchant marine, the fire-fighters and the Victorian Order of Nurses. Provision is made in this bill to extend the preference to those who served with the Y.M.C.A. and other auxiliary services, who really were not in the fighting services but were overseas doing work in hazardous positions. However I suggest that a Y.M.C.A. worker or a member of some other auxiliary service did not do any more exacting work and was not in a more dangerous position than members of the merchant marine or of the Victorian Order of Nurses, or even the fire-fighters. I believe very few of these are in the civil service, and perhaps not many of them would have to be considered, but there are those who have done their duty to their country in a notable way, and who, I believe, should be given considera-
Civil Service Act

tion when seeking positions in the civil service or when applying for promotions, and so on. Would the minister make a comment on this particular clause and state whether or not the government is willing to give them the status of veterans preference?

I do not intend to make a long speech on this bill. The veterans preference covered by this bill is the result of a recommendation made by the veterans affairs committee which sat last year. That committee recommended that the preference which had been provided during the war as a temporary measure be continued.

Did the veterans committee not state that it should be continued for the present, and was there not an expectation that a committee on the civil service would be set up this year to give further consideration to the matter of veterans preference? The committee on veterans affairs recommended that the preference remain as it was. I am sure the words "for the present" were in there because I looked them up only yesterday.

I am not sure of the wording, but I know that was the recommendation of the committee. I was gratified to receive today two letters from civil service organizations, one of which came to me only this evening from the acting president of the civil service federation, who states:
I thought you should know that the Civil Service Federation of Canada, at ah executive meeting held yesterday (Sunday) approved of the proposed amendments to the Civil Service Act and is anxious that they be adopted at the current session of parliament.
Then I have another letter from the national joint council of the public service of Canada. I do not want to pat myself on the back because I do not deserve it, but I want to read this letter, which is as follows:
The national joint council of the public service, having examined the provisions of the bill to amend the Civil Service Act,
(il) endorses the provisions of the bill;
(2)	expresses its appreciation of the action of the Secretary of State in facilitating its consideration of the bill;
(3)	expresses its appreciation of the work of the civil service commission, the Secretary of State and the government in connection with the bill; and
(4)	expresses the hope that the bill will be passed at the present session of parliament.
I read those letters so that they may be on the record. I appreciate the support of the bill that we have introduced which is given by these members of the civil service.

I do not think the minister answered the hon. member for Carleton who asked1 if it were possible to have the term "veteran" include a merchant seaman and members of the other services that were mentioned.

The matter was discussed by the veterans committee, and I would not take it upon myself to put it into the bill unless it came as a direct recommendation of the veterans committee. The Minister of Veterans Affairs suggested that next session the veterans committee might be reconvened and. of course, if that happened the matter would receive consideration.
I want to deal with the functioning of the civil service commission and I d'o not know whether I can do this on section 1 or section 2.
I think section 2 would be more appropriate.

I should like to appeal particularly to the members of the house who served on the special committee on veterans affairs which sat during 1945 and 1946. The minister was a member of that committee, out he was not able to attend very frequently. I am sure that from the beginning to the end of those sessions there was not one member of that committee who did not want to see merchant seamen treated as members of the fourth arm of the services. I do not think there was any sentiment against their being so treated. The minister has just suggested that he is not prepared to include them in this bill because there was no recommendation from that committee, but I think I can assure him that- no member of that committee is against the merchant seamen being given the civil service preference. If we delay until next year, the government will not want to open up the Civil Service Act, and that is easily understood. This is the time to set that matter right.
The merchant seamen are not getting the benefits given to the members of the other forces. Many who were disabled cannot get a pension under the present law and here is a case where they can be helped. I suggest that this preference be extended to cover them. It is merely a matter of extending the definition. Time and again, leaders across the country have taken the position that the merchant navy were the fourth arm of the services. I happen to have before me the speech from the throne, delivered on September 6, 1945, in which we find these words:
Our country will ever remember with pride the heroic exploits of Canada's fighting men and merchant seamen.

Civil Service Act
Here is a chance to do something for these men. I do not think there is one argument that can be advanced against extending preference to the men of the merchant navy. I ask the minister not to close the section without giving further consideration to amending it to include the men of the merchant navy. I appeal to those members who served on the veterans affairs committee to support us in in this respect. I am quite sure that there is not one of them who would have .the law other than including preference for the men of the merchant navy. Now is the time to come to their aid.

I want to support wholeheartedly what has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver South. During the sittings of the veterans committee I, along with many others, believed that the merchant seamen were going to get much more consideration than they have. Frequently benefits for merchant seamen have been requested by members on this side of the house, and I believe they had at least moral support from members on the other side. I could understand. though I could not justify, the government's reluctance to change this legislation if it meant that a great many more men were to come under pension and other benefits, but in this case it costs the government no more to hire a merchant seaman for a civil service job than it does to hire anybody else. I do not believe that the veterans organizations across Canada would oppose the inclusion of merchant seamen in the definition of those eligible for civil service positions. The government has no excuse whatsoever on the ground of costs for refusing to include them. The government might be afraid that this might be the opening wedge, which it will not be because I can assure them we shall persist in our attempts to get even further justifiable benefits for the merchant seamen of Canada. This question will be raised as long as there are veterans in this house and merchant seamen still alive, and the least the government can do is to give the merchant seamen partial recognition at least by including them in the definitions.

When speaking on the resolution, I showed, Mr. Chairman, that the French-speaking element makes up 30 per cent of our population and I mentioned that its representation in the oivil service was considerably below that percentage. I proved that in the civil service as a whole that percentage was very low. I wished to give certain details, but I was not permitted to do so.
I believe that it would be appropriate to give them now.
If we examine the various departments, from the first to the last, we find a shocking injustice in all ranks of civil servants. For example, out of twenty-two deputy ministers, not one is a French Canadian. The Montreal chamber of commerce made a complete investigation of the matter and drew up a very interesting table showing the proportion of French Canadians in the civil service, according to certain classifications. For example in the $8,000 yearly salary bracket and over, they note that the percentage of French Canadians is only 12-3 per cent, while the percentage of the French-speaking element makes up 30 per cent of the total population. Among employees earning $6,000 and over per annum, 8-12 represents the percentage of French Canadians, while among civil servants whose yearly salary is fixed at 54,000 and over, the proportion of Frenchspeaking citizens is estimated at 9'52 per cent. In the class earning a yearly salary of $3,000' and over, the percentage comes to 11-39 per cent while at the level of $2,400 and over per annum, which includes the largest number of ordinary employees, the proportion is found! to be 12-25 per cent.
Obviously, Mr. Chairman, French-speaking Canadians are not given their fair share of employment in the civil service. Why? It is claimed at times that they are not sufficiently qualified and that the reason why French Canadians do not have as much opportunity for promotion in the civil service is that they lack the required ability. Such an argument is not only extremely humiliating, but it is also ridiculous. First, what is meant by ability should be determined. How are qualifications decided upon? I find, for instance, that an ambassador was appointed deputy minister of mines. In what manner does an ambassador's post lead to that of deputy
Civil Service Act

minister of mines? On the other hand, the deputy minister of national revenue, a tax collector, has been elevated to the rank of ambassador. On what basis does the civil service commission or the government, judge ability?
Now, that argument may be open to question. It would be another matter if this unfairness towards French Canadians affected only a small number of employees from whom specialized scientific knowledge would be required; but that is not so, Mr. Speaker. Discrimination, as I have shown earlier, is found all along the line, in every department and in every branch. Now, it must further be assumed that in selecting Frenchspeaking candidates, the Civil Sendee Commission eagerly seeks those who offer the very least in the way of future possibilities. Further, it is ridiculous to claim that among three and one half million French Canadians, sufficiently qualified personnel required to fill even the $2,400 posts cannot, be found. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, the ability factor does not come into play.
What does all this bring about? I have shown that because of this discrimination towards French Canadians, my Frenchspeaking fellow-citizens lose $30 to $40 million per annum. If you add to that, Mr. Chairman, the fact that about 40 million dollars .are now being lost every year as a result of tax agreements between the dominion and the provinces, you will see that French-speaking Canadians will lose about 70 million dollars .each year.
Some are wondering why disunion exists in this country. Good will pilgrimages are *organized across Canada. Other provinces are told, for instance, that the reason why there is not understanding is that our schools are teaching that the deportation of Acadians occurred in 1755. I say that if there is disunion in this country it is not because our schools are teaching that the Acadians were deported in 1755, but rather because in 1947, and especially since 1919, the deportation of French Canadians from the civil service is going on systematically. That is the true cause of misunderstanding in this country.
Hear, hear.

Who are those responsible for that situation, Mr. Chairman? I notice the French representation in the civil service has sharply decreased especially since the creation of the civil service commisison. The chamlbre de commerce of Montreal, which gives us most interesting facta, shows for instance that in 1918 before the civil service commission as it now exists came into being,

our proportion was much greater than it is now. As regards the total number of positions in the country, our proportion was then 21-58 per cent, while it is now 12-25 per cent.
The downward trend has been particularly noticeable since the establishment of the civil service commission. Is that body responsible for such a state of affairs? I believe, Mr. Chairman, that it is not the only one to blame. However, it has its share of responsibility for the following reasons: first, it has given its approval to the so-called "made-to-measure requisitions" which have been so much ridiculed. A deputy minister or the head of a department wishes to have Mr. So-and-So appointed; he sets out himself the required qualifications and does so in such a way that only one person can meet the requirements, namely the one who has been chosen in advance and who quite often is already filling the position. Secondly, the responsibility of the civil service commission comes from the obligations it has under the act. The Civil Service Act places upon the commission, among others, the following duty:
Of its own motion to investigate and report upon the operation of this act and upon the violation of any of the provisions hereof or of any regulation made hereunder; and, upon the request of the head of a department, to investigate and report upon any matter relative to the department, its officers, clerks and other employees.
And besides:
To report upon the organization or proposed organization of the departments or any portion of any department or of the civil service, and upon any proposed change in such organization;
I respectfully submit, Mr. Chairman, that this clause of the Civil Service Act entrusts the commission with the duty to see that, in the civil service, the fundamental principle of our democracy "representation by population" is adhered to. The civil service commission has failed to do that and therefore bears full responsibility in the matter.
Now, Mr. Chairman, what reforms are indicated? I wonder whether the civil service commission is capable of making them. The first reform is to demand of every federal employee whose jurisdiction extends to the whole country that he be perfectly bilingual. What would be the result, I ask all hon. members of this house, if at a certain time one of them wishing to speak to the timber controller, for example, were to get the following answer; "I am sorry but I cannnot speak English." What could be the result of such a situation. If it is preposterous in the eyes of the English-speaking members, I respectfully submit that it is just as preposterous for French-speaking members.

Civil Service Act
Mr. Chairman, we are being told at times that, according to a school of thought now taking shape in the province of Quebec, the federal government is considered somewhat as a foreign government. It may be true. But who is to blame?
Take for instance the case of some constituent of mine who, coming to Ottawa and calling at various departments, finds that officials are exclusively English-speaking.
Here are a few instances: Veterans Affairs, out of four officials paid $8,000 or more, none are French-speaking. At the Department of Agriculture, out of five officials getting $8,000 or more, none are French-speaking. At the Department of Insurance, none. At the Auditor General's, none. At the Department of Commerce, none; at the Mutual Aid Board, none; at the Civil Service Commission, among those paid $8,000 or more yearly, none. I know there is a French-speaking commissioner, but he does get less than $8,000. At the National Research Council, none; at the Privy Council, none; at National Defence, out of four officials who get $8,000 or more, none are French-speaking. At the Department of Finance, out of four officials receiving a yearly salary of $8,000 or more, none are French speaking. At the Governor General's, none; at the Department of Justice, where three officials get $8,000 or more-those figures apply to 1946 and there may be one now, but of those three none are Frenchspeaking. At the National Film Board, none; Fisheries, nil; Reconstruction, not a single French-speaking official out of seven. At National Revenue, no French speaking official. A case in point would be as follows: A young man had just entered the civil service as a temporary employee. He was looking forward to being permanently employed later on. Under the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, the company would have to take this man back and give him the same position he had before. Under this bill, if he were employed as a temporary employee and came back from overseas, the government has no responsibility at all with regard to taking him on. This
section deals with extending the privilege which was granted after the first world war to veterans of the second war. During the first war. permanent employees who had resigned and joined the forces were not automatically taken back into the service and they were not granted the privilege of coming back to their employment. But after the war was over, they were reinstated. Early in this war, in order to prevent the permanents from resigning and going overseas, they were told they would not be reinstated at the end of the war. However I think better judgment was displayed later. Those who had permanent positions before the war now have the right of being brought back to the service, but in many cases the positions for them are not available. For example, a man does not come back and resume the permanent position he had before the war.' As will be understood, it being a permanent position, when the man resigned the position was filled. The result is that the man who resigned applies to the commission to be reinstated in the civil service and the commission places his name on the list of eligible persons. Then, when there is a vacancy he is entitled to be taken back to a position of the same kind as that from which he had resigned. I quite agree with my hon. friend that this does not specifically provide for temporary employees. A man who resigned from his temporary position is entitled, when he comes back, to take a position for which he is qualified, but I admit that this forces the commission to place his name on the eligible list.

The ordinary rules of procedure have been broken and the order of business interfered with. It is not a question of whether the minister will protect the rights of the hon. member tomorrow. We all saw the hon. member standing on his feet and calling to Mr. Speaker, but Mr. Speaker deliberately ignored him, walked from the chair and left the chamber. That is a serious matter. It is something that should be righted now if there is any way in which it can be done.
We have drawn the attention of the house to the matter, and1 I would be very much pleased and think it would be better if we now let the matter drop.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
As leader of the house, I cannot for one second permit any reflection on the Speaker. I have the greatest personal admiration for him, for his conduct of business in this house and for his fairness to all parties. If something happened tonight, things sometimes happen quickly without anyone being responsible for it, and' I am sure it was not the fault of the Speaker. I, as leader of the house, at once accept full responsibility that the hon. member for Dauphin was not seen on his feet, and I assure my hon. friend that he will have ample opportunity to speak tomorrow.
Demobilization and reconversion-
583. Departmental administration, $7-2,740.
Will the minister explain this item? It comes under demobilization and reconversion. I should like to know for what purpose the money is being voted.

It has to do with the administration arising out of demobilization. During the war we had certain administrative services in the Department of Transport having exclusively to do with war. The vote is gradually go-ing down. It has to do with demobilizing these services.
There is an increase this year over last. What are the services performed in this connection?

There is transport control, for instance, which is being wound up;
nautical services; compensation for loss of effects; joint Canada-United States defence.
What is that?

That is a service we shall discuss in a moment. It was set up during the war to purchase property on behalf of the United States government. That is now being wound1 up. It also operated and disposed: of property. This service was established in the Department of Transport for other departments.

I wish to draw to the minister's attention that vote 583 for $72,740 comprises an item of $66,700 for temporary assistance. All through the estimates of the Department of Transport there are items for temporary assistance, totalling eight or nine million dollars. It is very hard to get a satisfactory answer from any minister to the question, what is temporary assistance?

So far as this item is
concerned, there cannot be much difficulty because this was a non-continuing service and. of necessity had to be -temporary. That is why it is so described in the details.

Item agreed to.

585. Director of merchant seamen, $425,340.

This is a vote of nearly
half a million dollars. Is any provision being made for the training of merchant seamen for the future?

Provision is made for
vocational training within the seamen's calling.

I do not mean that. The
Minister of Reconstruction explained very fully a few weeks ago that Canada proposed to maintain a merchant navy of considerable size. Is any plan in effect for training the personnel for that merchant marine? We had such a plan during the war and quite a few thousand men were trained for the merchant navy. Has such policy been dropped, or are we going to have any facilities for training these men for our merchant marine?

During the war we
had two schools, one at Prescott for engineering and one at St. Margarets, Nova Scotia. Both were set up specifically for the training of merchant seamen during the war. These two schools have been discontinued. There are, however, a number of schools such as existed prior to the war, as for instance, the marine technical training school at Prescott; school of navigation, Vancouver;

the Hopkins School of Engineering, Vancouver; government navigation school, Halifax; dominion navigation school, Yarmouth; and vocational training such as I mentioned a moment ago. At the schools men receive training for engineering and seamanship generally.
These facilities could train only a few men.
A limited number.

Is the government accepting any responsibility for training the personnel that will be required to man the Canadian merchant navy? In the United Kingdom I believe they have regular training schools for the merchant navy, and probably the same thing is true of the United' States. It does . seem reasonable that Canada should have some provisions of the same kind. We cannot continue to keep an efficient merchant marine without efficient personnel. New men will be coming in all the time. What facilities are there, if any, for giving that training?

I can only repeat what I said a moment ago. During the war we had the two schools mentioned, and we have closed them down. There are no facilities for training merchant seamen now. I know that at the I.L.O. convention in Seattle a recommendation was made to the effect that certain groups of the navy should1 be certified. If that recommendation is approved-
Certain groups of what?

Certain groups of the merchant seamen should be certified as cooks, able-bodied seamen and other groups such as boatswains and so forth. If that convention is ratified, then we shall have to set up schools here.
Will the dominion accept the full responsibility for providing facilities for training?
If the convention is approved I presume that- will follow.
The minister referred1 to a number of schools. Are these schools carried on under the auspices of the Department of Transport?
No.
Are they private schools?
They are not carried on under our auspices, but we subsidize them.
They are private schools subsidized by the Department of Transport?

They are provincial
schools assisted and subsidized by the Department of Transport.
What is meant by "provincial schools"? Does that mean schools under the provincial government?
Not necessarily; it means schools within the province such as the one I referred to at Prescott, a marine technical school. I think I spoke of a school of navigation at Vancouver.
Can the minister give us any idea of the number of students in these schools at the present time?

I cannot give the
information now. I shall have to get. it by communicating with the directors of these schools. I can get it for my hon. friend.

Has the minister any
information as to the number of seamen in Canada now unemployed, if any? I am not suggesting that there are any.

From the position as I know it, I would think there are very few because there is a great demand for seamen.
Mr. HERRIIX3E: What are the duties of the director of merchant seamen?
May I be allowed to answer the previous question? I am informed that at the moment we are paying out-of-work benefits to fifty unemployed seamen.

Can the minister explain briefly the duties of the director of merchant
seamen?

The director of merchant seamen had important duties during the war. He was responsible for the manning of merchant ships; he was responsible for the manning pools, the schools that were set up, the various bonuses that were paid and so on. Now that the war has come to an end, there are a number of benefits to which merchant seamen are entitled and which must be adman,istered by the department. They are administered by the department through the director of merchant, seamen. For instance, there is a war service bonus of ten per cent paid1 to certain groups of merchant seamen who served in dangerous waters. That bonus is paid through the office of the director. Likewise there is a special war service bonus which is also paid through him. Vocational training for merchant seamen is under his direction, and the claims for detention allowances, claims by merchant seamen who lost their effects, or by dependents of merchant seamen who lost

Supply-Transport
their effects, some of which are still coming in, are under the direction of the director of merchant seamen. His duties are, I must say, diminishing considerably.
Mr. MacIX.MS: Do the out-of-work benefits which the minister referred to a moment ago come under the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act?

No, it is a different thing altogether. This comes under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Mr. MacI X XI,S: For persons who had war service ?
That is correct. They are put in the same category in so far as unemployment insurance is concerned as the members of the armed forces.
Do the provinces have a director of merchant seamen?
Xo.
Who is in charge of the manning pools?
They were under the direction of the director of merchant seamen during the war, but they have now been closed.
They are not active now?
Xo.
How many men are there in the merchant navy at the present time?
About fifteen thousand.
Who looks after the merchant seamen in the province of British Columbia? Apparently veterans affairs have disowned them.

In so far as their employment and discharge are concerned, the shipping master at the port of Vancouver looks after them. In so far as their benefits under these various orders in council are concerned, it is the director of merchant seamen.

Apparently veterans affairs have disowned, them. If they have a complaint in British Columbia, do they have to bring it to Ottawa? Is there nobody in that Pacific coast port to whom they can take their complaint?
They are referred by the various seamen's organizations across Canada to the director of merchant seamen.
In other words, they have to go to their unions and the union has to take it up by indirect control with Ottawa; is that correct?
Not necessarily the unions. There are many groups looking after merchant seamen who are not unionized or organized.
The federal government has no representative in the main coast port of British Columbia?

My department has many representatives on the Pacific coast, but not all of them deal with merchant seamen. They deal with various matters. A moment ago I referred to the shipping master who has to do with engaging and discharge of merchant seamen, the registration of seamen and so on. The supervisor of nautical services has these responsibilities under his control.

What I am trying to get at is this. If a merchant seaman on the Pacific coast has a complaint, veterans affairs have told me tonight that they disown him entirely; has that merchant seaman any recourse ?
I am afraid I have to disagree with the hon. member. The Minister of Veterans Affairs did not. say that the department had disowned merchant seamen.

I do not agree
with the minister and he does not agree with me. What recourse has a merchant seaman on the Pacific coast? Who does he approach with his complaint? Does he have to come to Ottawa?

I should like to know
to what my hon. friend is referring. If he will give me an example of the complaint he has in mind, perhaps I cart give him a more definite answer.
Suppose a merchant seaman considers that he was unjustly treated in the merchant marine.

If he considers that
he has not received a bonus or has not received the benefits to which he was entitled, what I suppose he would do would be to complain to the minister. I have received some such complaints and the Minister of Veterans Affairs has received a number of such complaint*. If he is referring to matters dealing with nautical service or with registration, then I presume he would make his complaint to the shipping master in the port where he is stationed.

The minister has
surmised correctly what I meant, but what I wish to know is this. Is there no means on the Pacific coast cf dealing with his

application? Is it necessary that he should have to go through all the red tape at Ottawa in order to present his case?

He makes his complaint through his organization in the. port where he resides, whether it be the west coast seamen's union or the Canadian seamen's union or the seamen's welfare society if he is in Montreal. There are various organizations in all parts of Canada, and if he has a complaint to make he can complain directly to the minister or through one of these organizations.
Montreal is a long way from Vancouver. My question is this: Have you no representative in your department in Vancouver?
I have already told the hon. gentleman that there are several representatives of my department in the port of Vancouver.

Are we clear as to who is
responsible for the merchant seamen? We have had a good illustration tonight of the difficulties of getting fair treatment for merchant seamen. They are involved in the two departments of transport and veterans affairs, and I do not believe they will get justice until it is decided which department is responsible for them. The minister said on July 2, at page 5001 of Hansard:
I wish someone would clear up in my mind and to my satisfaction whose responsibility this is.
Hear, hear.

I feel exactly like the
minister. I should like to know whose responsibility this is, because the Minister of Veterans Affairs promised the other day that next year a special committee on veterans affairs would be set up again. This injustice will be brought up in that committee, certainly if I am a member of it, and I am sure that the hon. member for Fraser Valley would take the same view. There are certain injustices to be considered, such as failure to give these men pensions for disabilities, failure to provide vocational training, and failure to give the benefits of the Veterans Land Act and many other benefits. Who is to be responsible for them-transport or veterans affairs? We should like to know, because wrhen we sit on that committee next year the whole question will be gone into thoroughly and someone will have to answer all the questions that are asked. We are not going to fall between two stools as we did last year.
[Mr. Cruickahank.l

I am afraid I shall not be the one to answer those questions. However I will answer the first part of the question my hon. friend asks, when he wishes to know what the responsibility of this department is. In so far as the engagement and discharge of seamen, the amount of payment due, and so forth are concerned, that has been the responsibility of the Department of Transport through the shipping master in the various ports. In so far as benefits approved by the government under various orders in council are concerned., they have thus far ben under the administration of the director of merchant seamen. That far I can go, but beyond that I cannot.
There is one item of 197,040 for vocational training, but that means only vocational training for merchant seamen who want to go to sea.
Yes.
Those who do not want to go back to sea do not get such training?
They are not covered by the order in council.
Then I am correct in putting it that way.
You are correct.

If a recommendation is made next year by the veterans affairs committee that these men should get vocational training apart from training to fit them to go to sea, or that they should get the benefit of university grants, such recommendations would have to be carried out by the Department of Transport?

Not necessarily. The government would then have to decide whether the recommendations should be carried out by the veterans affairs department or the director of merchant seamen. It may be that next year the latter may not exist. I do not know.

I do not know whether this discussion is in order, but I have listened to the hon. member for Vancouver South on several occasions making a plea for merchant seamen who were in the merchant navy during the war. I too have said a little on the subject, but I felt that, as the matter was being discussed, we could not get anywhere in a debate of this kind. My feelinig is that the government must decide where the responsibility rests. They should refer it to the veterans affairs committee if they think these men have service comparable with that of men in the armed service as I believe they

Supply-Transport
have. I suggest that the question, should be referred to the committee on veterans affairs and have it decided once and for all, so that we can get away from this discussion.

I have the greatest appreciation of the hon. member for Vancouver East, but I would point out that the hon. member for Vancouver South and I were vocal on this point last year when we tried as members of the veterans affairs committee to have it decided. Every member of that committee will bear me out when I say that we were two members who were vocal on the point. We fought this matter and we are not now satisfied as to who is responsible.

This is about the sixth debate I have heard on the question of injustice to merchant seamen. Let us analyse the question of the merchant seamen. He was a civilian doing a hard and dangerous job. He had always been a civilian free to work or to stop work. He got special bonuses for going into dangerous situations. But there were other dangerous jobs in the country. I could mention one where the percentage of loss in a civilian job was higher than it was among merchant seamen, and that is among men in commercial transport service, the operators who ferried new planes across the Atlantic.
That is another complaint we have. Those men are not protected either.
They were not as numerous as the merchant seamen.
And they are not protected.

Now here were men doing a civilian job. It is true that some of them went into dangerous waters, while others did not. I know about the work of the merchant seamen because I have suffered with them, and I know how tough it is, but I am not prepared to say that a man who did not put on a uniform, who did not sign up for a term of duty, who did not place himself in the position where he would have to go into a dangerous stiuation when he was so ordered, is in the same position as the veteran who wore the uniform. My hon. friend contends that he is. I am not even prepared to agree that the terms of reference to the veterans affairs committee extend to men who did not serve in uniform. The position of the merchant seaman has been well taken care of. He is not a man who was put out of his job when the war ended. There are more jobs for Canadian merchant seamen today than at any time during the war, and there will be more jobs five years hence, or at any rate three years hence, than there are today.
Seamanship is a trade like any other. My hon. friend might as well ask who was responsible for carpenters. The man responsible for carpenters, as far as the government is concerned, is the Minister of Labour, and the Minister of Labour is responsible for merchant seamen. The merchant seaman has a union which is well able to protect his interests, and he has the Minister of Labour to arbitrate in any differences he may have with the government.
It seems to me that we are wasting a great deal of sympathy to men well able to take care of themselves. The wages of merchant seamen have increased more as a result of the war than the wages in any other line that I know of. These men have kept all their wartime gains and bonuses and have had two or three substantial increases since the war ended. I would say that the merchant seamen of Canada are in an excellent position today and they have a future which few other tradesmen in this country can look forward to.
I am amazed that a responsible minister of the crown would take an attitude like that.
What is the other attitude? The poor downtrodden merchant seamen!
Just sit still and listen.

I have been listening for
weeks.

Right from His Majesty down, responsible leaders of the democratic nations have taken the position that the men in the merchant navy were the fourth arm of the service, and quite properly so. The minister's own leader, the Prime Minister of this country, just two or three days ago, on Dominion day, praised them and treated them as though they were members of the armed service. Now the Minister of Reconstruction stands up in this house and says they were just the same as a carpenter working on land.
He did not say any such thing.
I did not say anything of the kind. May I ask the hon. member not to carry his prejudices so far as to put words into my mouth?

He said that they are not entitled to any special consideration. I would point out to him the fact that there were thousands of young men, and older men too, who went into the merchant navy to do their bit in the war.

Yes.
