They were not regular merchant seamen. They do not want to go back to sea now that the war is over. They went in there to do their bit. Perhaps they were not eligible physically to go into the army. They did a grand job. They suffered many casualties. 1 think the casualties in the Canadian merchant marine were heavier in proportion than those of all the other three arms of the service. If the minister talks for ten years, he cannot tell me that a merchant navy man who was crippled for life by falling on a ship in the blackout, say in Liverpool, is not entitled to any pension.
I am not trying to say that.

That is the position the Canadian merchant seaman finds himself in today. He is not covered for that. He gets pension only where he suffered by reason of direct enemy action. In the same way a young lad from Vancouver not even waiting until he is eighteen-even at sixteen and seventeen they went into the merchant navy- gets a tropical disease. His health is ruined for life, and he can get no compensation under our present law. Nobody can tell me that is fair. Nobody can tell me it is fair that a young man who served in dangerous waters with the merchant navy has to pay his way through a Canadian university when a boy who served only in Canada in the army gets his way paid. Having listened to the minister, we have probably now got the reason that it is so hard to get justice for these men. The Canadian Legion welcomes them to membership on the same basis as a' member of the navy, the army or the air force. Without exception, the members of the veterans affairs committee treated them as though they were in the same category as men who served in any of the other forces.
Almost.

The hon. member for Fraser Valley will bear me out in that. There is not a member of the veterans affairs committee who will get up and deny that statement. We are trying to see that they get a fair deal. Apparently they fell between the two departments. the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of Transport; and they are still falling between those two departments. We believe they have had a raw deal and we want to see that they get a fair deal. It does not matter what the Minister of Reconstruction says. In my opinion, he is wrong again, just as he has been wrong on many other occasions in the past few years.
Will my hon. friend tell me what country gives the type of treatment which he proposes? Does Britain or the United States give it?
What is that?
What country gives to merchant seamen the same benefits as they give to their troops?
I am not interested in what other countries do.
No, evidently not
We hear the Minister of Veterans Affairs-
Everybody is wrong but the hon. member for Vancouver South.
Well, sometimes.
Quite often.

This is one time when we are all right except the minister of reconstruction. We hear so much in this house about the benefits for the veterans being so fine in Canada, and their being better here than they are anywhere else in the world.
That is right.

They are still not good enough. There are many things still to be remedied with regard to benefits for Veterans. We cannot see why the merchant seamen should not be put in the same position. I warn the government that sooner or later it will have to be done; because if it is not forced on them by the opposition it will be forced on them from their own back benches. Sooner or later this thing must be faced. I would suggest that some thought be given to it in the interval between this session and the next one.

I should like to say one word in reply to what the minister said. Apparently everyone except the merchant seamen got the O.B.E. or the M.B.E. All you had to do was to serve as a dollar-a-year man in Sore] or somewhere else, making a fortune, and you got the O.B.E. or something. I want to tell the minister that it is all poppycock to tell me that the salary we pay to merchant seamen is adequate compensation, and nobody knows it better than the minister; he himself was sunk in the middle of the Atlantic. The fact that we have done so much does not answer the question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I am surprised, and I think some of the legionnaires will be surprised, that the membsrs of the veterans

We could not get anywhere because we were told the matter was going to be raised under another branch. We were told it would be brought up under another department when we insisted that equal treatment be accorded members of the merchant marine. To tell me that they got extra pay is no answer. If this man suffers one iota as a result of my mentioning his name, his condition, and the way he has been treated, I shall be very sorry. And the minister tells me that they get extra pay-

speechtext: I never told you that.
*-in the merchant marine. I feel bitter about that merchant marine. I think they got a dirty deal.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I absolutely resent that remark. It is not true. It is a falsification of the facts. They did not get a dirty deal. They got a very generous deal in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Vancouver South or the hon. member for Vancouver East made me retract one time. I think that is hardly parliamentary.

I should not like this debate to conclude without saying a word; and if my intrusion is resented by the last speaker, perhaps he will realize that more than anyone else he invited it, in spite of the fact that the other day in the committee he told me I talked too much. There can be no doubt that in the veterans affairs committee of last year consideration of the claims of the merchant seamen were set aside from our deliberations because the committee understood that the whole question of merchant seamen, excluding the civil service preference which was within a different department, was being considered by the Department of Transport. We were not told that the transport department was going to provide benefits paralleling the veterans benefits, but our understanding clearly was that certain benefits were being considered for merchant seamen and that our committee, which was to deal strictly with veterans' matters, should await the decision on that legislation before entering into the discussion.

I have forgotten the date, but I believe it was about February 12 when a sub-committee of the veterans affairs committee was set up, of which I had the honour to be chairman, and we were asked to consider such benefits accruing to Canadian veterans of the last war as might be applied to those who had served in a civilian capacity during the war, and the extent to which our committee would be prepared to recommend that these veterans benefits be extended. At that time the terms of reference to the sub-committee expressly excluded from our consideration the large question of the merchant seamen, and that sub-committee did not report on merchant seamen except with respect to those benefits, limited in number and chiefly with respect to pensions and other benefits which would accrue to merchant seamen who had become pensionable through being injured in action or in evasive action, which had already been announced.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Fourteen in all.

I do not remember the
number, but subsequently they were extended and I am told they now number fourteen. It is not correct to say, as was said in the house some time ago, that the veterans affairs committee expected that transport would deal with the question, for instance, which was up a little while ago; that is, the matter of the veterans preference. It was realized then that this would have to be part of the larger picture, on which the committee did not make a recommendation last year; and I presume, in fact I know, it will be a part of that larger picture when these things come up again. But in my view it is not fair to say, as was said here tonight, that the committee was misled, that the committee was told the merchant seamen were being taken care of and, by implication, that we in the veterans affairs committee did not need to make a recommendation. Quite frankly, I do not think a suggestion of that kind would have been swallowed by that committee or by any member of it.
The record is clear. The statement in that regard, if I remember rightly, was made by the chairman of that committee, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who told us quite frankly that the matter was under consideration by the Department of Transport as to what benefits were to be given, and by implication I think we all understood that, should our committee feel the recommendations of the Department of Transport did not adequately meet the case-and certainly many members of the committee now feel that they do not meet the case-we would have an opportunity of

considering them specifically. That, I think, is an honest and fair picture of what took place then. When the committee Tose after some fifty-one sittings, and I do not know how many sub-committee meetings, there was still no definite programme before the committee from the transport department with respect to merchant seamen; and I think in the mind of every member of the committee the situation with respect to merchant seamen and such war benefits as should accrue to them was and is unfinished business.

I feel I should say just one word, and I would not do so but for what was stated a moment ago. I do not want to repeat, but this matter has been gone over frequently this session; I think this is the third debate we have had thus far on merchant seamen. I am sorry it has to take place, but I feel that I should place the position of the Department of Transport clearly before the committee once more, for the third time. I, as minister, certainly had no understanding as to what was being done by the committee on veterans affairs, nor did I or my officers have any such understanding as was stated here. I have to repeat that statement in fairness to the officers of my department. I did have in mind bringing down a bill, which I brought down later, concerning compensation to merchant seamen. That was in the nature of workmen's compensation, for injuries arising out of the nature of the occupation.
And only post-war.

Yes, beginning in 1945.
That was the only thing I had in mind. Over and above that was the question of unemployment insurance to merchant seamen. There was the matter of vocational training for merchant seamen in their own calling, and there was one other matter which slips my mind at the moment. Those were the things for which I was responsible, which I brought before this house and which received the approval of the house. Beyond that I know nothing of what took place in the veterans affairs committee. So I wonder if we could not get along with these estimates and particularly with this item. We have had three or four debates on it this session.

The Minister of Veterans Affairs has said that he attended the meetings of the committee quite regularly. In order to end this debate, since we are now discussing the Department of Transport, if ini his opinion the merchant seamen are not receiving fair treatment, why does he not, as Minister of Veterans Affairs, get up in the house and

Supply-Transport
briefly express his opinion, and say he will try to work on his colleague the Minister of Transport to see that the merchant seamen are looked after as in his opinion, speaking as a veteran, they should be looked after.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am not going to accept an undeserved rebuke from an hon. member who is sadly misinformed about this whole situation. I have been working on this problem for thirty long years; I have given my whole life to it. I know the problem of the merchant seamen; I know what England has done for them; I know what Canada has done for them; and if my hon. friend knew the facts he would be proud of what Canada has done for them in comparison with any other country in the world. If he is trying to dragoon or bludgeon me into any admission of failure he is talking to the wrong man, I can tell him. I will have the policy outlined as the government may determine that policy. That is the Liberal doctrine. The Tories might have one minister declare a policy for himself, but not the Liberal government; because we are a collective agency of democratic independence. Our policy is prepared by our spokesmen for the party, and by those policies we stand always.

Did I understand the minister to say this is the Liberal doctrine and the Liberal way of carrying out these matters? He has not yet stated his personal opinion as a veteran, as to whether he thinks this is fair treatment. That is a precise question, which should receive a precise answer.
What did the Tory government do for them after the first war?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They sent them to slave camps.
I can speak as one who had over four years of service-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I tell my hon. friend that our record in regard to the veterans will far outshine anything the Tories ever did for them.

As a veteran of four and a half years of service in the first war, I can say I believe I received everything I was entitled to. I did not fight in the hope of getting a pension. I considered it a privilege to fight for my country. I tried to do it again in this war, even going so far as to dye my hair.
Answer the question.
I will answer it. I think the Tory party gave the veterans all they were entitled to. We did not try to buy votes one way or the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You did not get them, anyway.
Is the past going to run the country? You say the Tory party never did anything. Is that any reason why you should do nothing?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You never did anything for the merchant seamen in all your existence.
You say we did nothing, and neither will you. Is that your answer?

We had a large number of members of the air force, the army and navy in our city during the war. This item 585 covers the director of merchant seamen. There is an item of $70,000 a year to extend for eight years, or a total of $560,000 for lifesaving. Why should the city of Toronto go all over the great lakes to do the work of the Department of Transport? There are no lifesaving stations on the great lakes on the Canadian side. I asked the minister on his main estimates what they proposed to do about setting up a national life-saving system on the great lakes. All the money for this purpose is spent on the gulf and on the oceans. Will the minister make a reply before the transport items are finished?

The hon. gentleman's question is not within the scope of this item, but I shall give him the information he wants. On the main estimates he asked what lifesaving equipment and appliances we had on the great lakes. There are on the great lakes between Kingston and the Canadian-United States border near Fort William, 426 light stations, fog-alarm plants and light and signal buoys and, in addition thereto, there are approximately 1,100 unlighted buoys, beacons, et cetera. Also, there are seven ship to shore radio telegraph and telephone stations to provide constant 24-hour communication with ships on all the great lakes. These stations regularly broadcast weather forecasts, storm warnings and notices of dangers to navigation. There are also fifteen automatic radio beacons from which ships take their bearings by radio. Over and above that, a number of ships are equipped with special appliances such as radar equipment, which is of great assistance in combating weather conditions.

When a ship on the Canadian side is in trouble it must sound its siren and wait for the United States life-saving station to send out help.

Marine service-
587. Nautical service, $106,450.

Part of this vote is to cover the repatriation of Canadian merchant seamen prisoners of war. Some of these merchant seamen who were prisoners have been brought back by the Canadian government and charged their fares.
I am informed by the director who is here that there are none. If my hon. friend has any cases I wish he would give them to me.
I have a case right here which I will place before the minister privately, in which a man was charged $423.38 repatriation expenses.
If the hon. member will give me the particulars I will look into the matter. I am sure there must be some error.
All these men were brought back by the government?
That is right.
And they are not supposed to be charged for their repatriation?
Not if they come under the description of a merchant seaman prisoner of war.
How wide is that description?
It covers the personnel of Canadian ships and Canadian seamen on other ships as well.
Would it apply to a Canadian who served on an allied ship?
Yes. If the hon. member will send over the case I shall be glad to look into it.

How much has been paid under this item altogether?
Can the minister give the same information for the next item?
,|Mr. Chevrier.]

On my return from Steep Rock, I was informed that they were held up because of a lack of cars, and I should like to know if this company is now able to get all the cars it requires to send out its ore?

They are not able to get all the cars they require, but they are in a better position than they have been at any time because of the cars they have on lease and1 the new cars that are being purchased by the Canadian National Railways.

I want to bring to the minister's notice the unsatisfactory train service on the Canadian National Railways between Calgary and Edmonton. 1 had occasion to bring this to his notice last session and I believe it was referred to the railway board. At that time I compared the service on the Canadian National with that on the Canadian Pacific. On the Canadian Pacific they have three trains each way each day and, besides, there is a paved highway and a good bus service. On the Canadian National there is one train south one day and then the train goes north the next, so that they get a train every other day. There is no paved highway and no bus service. My constituents feel that they are entitled to at least one train a day in each direction, which is what they used to have before the war. This was discontinued, and they feel there should be at least one train a day each way. I might give an instance. If a person wanted to go to Edlmonton for some function on Saturday evening he would have to start on Thursday afternoon and he could not get back to Mirror until Monday afternoon. I trust that the minister will take that into consideration.

Yes. If I might take one moment to reply to my hon. friend, it is true, as he says, that the service on the Canadian Pacific is excellent and that there is a difference between their service and that on the Canadian National, the reason being that the Canadian National railway between Edmonton and Calgary has a mileage of 232, as opposed to 194 for the Canadian Pacific, and the population along the Canadian National line is much smaller than along the Canadian Pacific and the traffic much lighter. Those are the reasons for the difference in service. I drew the situation to which the hon. member refers to the attention of the management of the Canadian National rail-

ways. I wrote him at some length on it, but in view of my hon. friend's added representations I shall be glad to take the matter up with them again.
We do not expect a service similar to that on the Canadian Pacific railway because they have three trains each way each day. All we ask is one train each way each day.
